articles.title: Toward Reproducible Research with LLMs: Guidance for Documentation, Reporting, and Transparency
articles.authors: Ryan Watkins; Vicky W. Lee
articles.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into scientific research workflows across many disciplines, creating new opportunities for literature review, research design, data analysis, simulation, coding, automation, and other forms of scientific inquiry. Their growing use also creates challenges for transparency and reproducibility, particularly because LLM outputs are nondeterministic, model capabilities change rapidly, and research workflows may involve multiple models, agents, tools, and computational environments. This guide proposes a framework and checklist for systematically documenting and reporting the use of LLMs as scientific instruments. Grounded in the principle that documentation requirements should be proportional to the methodological role of the LLM and its potential impact on research findings, the framework distinguishes among varying levels of human agency, methodological impact, and corresponding documentation needs. We provide guidance for determining what aspects of a LLM-enabled research workflow should be documented, how thoroughly they should be reported, and how those requirements change as the methodological role of AI increases. We further distinguish between documentation collected throughout the research process and information reported in manuscripts and supplementary materials. Rather than treating reproducibility as requiring identical LLM outputs, we emphasize sufficient methodological transparency to enable others to understand, evaluate, and, where desirable and feasible, reproduce or systematically test the research workflow and its results. The proposed guidance is intended to support researchers, reviewers, editors, and disciplinary communities as norms for transparent and reproducible LLM use continue to evolve.

articles.title: Disordered Eating and Risk Factors Across Sexual Minority Men’s Tribe Identities
articles.authors: Orestis Michaelides; Lyndsey Wallace
articles.abstract: Sexual minority men experience disproportionately high rates of disordered eating. Recent work has shown that within this population, levels of disordered eating may vary across men who identify with different tribes, a set of identities centered around the body and physical appearance. This study investigated whether tribes have a unique association with disordered eating, or whether they reflect variation in two known risk factors that show theoretical relevance to these subcultural identities, i.e., body surveillance and internalized homophobia. Data from 349 sexual minority men showed that the endorsement of several tribe identities (Twinks, Jocks, Otters) was related to internalized homophobia and age. Results additionally showed that when controlling for these known risk factors, tribe identities still captured unique variance in disordered eating: men who identified as Bears or Cubs showed greater disordered eating, while men who identified as Twinks showed less disordered eating relative to men without a tribe identity. Collectively, these findings suggest that tribes have a nuanced role in men’s relationships with their body and sexual minority identity, and the link between tribes and disordered eating is underpinned by different psychological mechanisms than what has been previously suggested.

articles.title: Towards an Integrative, Interdisciplinary, and Multidimensional Approach to Curbing Epistemically Suspect Beliefs: A Commentary on Bronstein et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Magdalena Adamus; Jais Adam-Troian; Maria Chayinska
articles.abstract: In this commentary, we endorse the recent call by Bronstein et al. (2026) to open a polyphonic debate and bring clinical psychology into the dialogue on the nature, causes, and consequences of epistemically suspect beliefs. We concur with the authors’ call for creating an integrative approach that would triangulate findings across different disciplines in a much-needed attempt to harmonise knowledge about individual, situational, and structural factors that contribute to the endorsement of epistemically suspect beliefs. Using economic anxiety as a model case, we then show how the integration of clinical insights could inform innovative, cost-effective, and scalable intervention programmes. Finally, we call for careful consideration of the risks associated with incorporating the clinical perspective, particularly the potential pathologisation of epistemically suspect beliefs and stigmatisation of those who endorse them, as well as the need to carefully distinguish delusions from ill-informed beliefs and rational suspicions.

articles.title: Missing Pretest–Posttest Correlations in Pretest–Posttest–Control Group Designs:  A Practical Trade-Off for Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Lucas Wilhelm Liebenow; Valentin Emslander; Thorben Jansen; Oliver Lüdtke
articles.abstract: Pretest–posttest–control group (PPC) effect sizes incorporate baseline information but require the pretest–posttest correlation for sampling-variance estimation, which is frequently unavailable in primary studies. This creates a practical trade-off: retaining baseline information requires an assumption about repeated-measures dependence, whereas using posttest-only effect sizes avoids this requirement but discards available baseline information. The present study used a simulation to evaluate whether missing correlations can be replaced by constant assumed values while maintaining acceptable variance calibration, and complemented the simulation with reanalyses of three published meta-analyses to illustrate the consequences for meta-analytic effects. Across 2,160 design conditions, we examined the sampling variances of two pretest-informed estimators (dppc1  and dppc2). Performance was evaluated in terms of coverage of nominal 95% confidence intervals and standard-error ratios. Across the fixed-correlation conditions, coverage declined from .97 to .83 for dppc1 and from .97 to .79 for dppc2 as the assumed correlation increased from .20 to .80, with corresponding standard-error ratios declining from 1.31 to 0.70 and from 1.32 to 0.68. Misspecification was asymmetric: overestimating the true correlation produced anti-conservative standard errors and undercoverage, whereas underestimating it generally produced conservative inference. Across the empirical examples, pooled PPC estimates were comparatively stable across correlation assumptions, whereas ignoring baseline information produced larger shifts in several pooled effects.  Based on these findings, we provide practical guidelines for handling missing pretest–posttest correlations, emphasizing a hierarchical use of study-specific information, external evidence, and transparent sensitivity analyses when constant assumptions are required. An accompanying Shiny app supports these analyses: https://lliebenow.shinyapps.io/ppc-rho-sensitivity-explorer/.

articles.title: Predictors Associated with Early Career Researcher Wellbeing: A Systematic Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sophie Fletcher; Amber Tout; Talar Moukhtarian; Tabitha Jackson; Chloe Mitchell; Elena Riva; Carla Toro; Marie Sams; Sotaro Kita
articles.abstract:
Objective: Early Career Researchers (ECRs) are integral to the academic ecosystem, representing a critical window for mental health promotion and early intervention within the higher education workforce. Their wellbeing is influenced by various factors that can either support or hinder healthy professional and personal development. This systematic scoping review maps and narratively synthesises current literature to understand predictors of ECR wellbeing, with the aim of informing upstream strategies for prevention and mental health promotion. 
Method: A systematic search was conducted across Web of Science, PsycINFO, and EBSCO (inception–May 2024). Of 2,577 records retrieved, 68 articles (69 independent studies) were included after screening.
Results: Seventeen distinct predictor clusters were identified and grouped by who has the most agency over them: 1) ECRs, 2) labs and departments, 3) institutions, 4) the sector, 5) all levels of agents combined. Frequently explored predictors included personal characteristics (i.e., age, gender), supervisor support and work-life balance, while depression, anxiety and stress were the most frequently measured outcomes.
Discussion: This review highlights both systemic and modifiable risk factors of occupational and psychological distress among ECRs. By identifying key drivers of wellbeing, this review offers actionable insights for developing early, targeted interventions at multiple levels. Investing in preventative and promotive strategies during this formative career stage may not only protect the wellbeing of ECRs but also foster healthier, more productive and sustainable academic environments.

articles.title: Understanding Creativity in Human–AI Collaboration:  How Cognitive Strategies and Student Profiles Relate to Students’ Creativity
articles.authors: Kim van Broekhoven; Marian Hickendorff
articles.abstract: Creativity is widely recognized as a critical competency for addressing the complex challenges of the twenty-first century. At the same time, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how students learn, think, and solve problems in higher education. In human-AI collaboration, this study first identified students’ cognitive strategies in GenAI-supported contexts, and examined the relationship between the cognitive strategy used and the creativity (i.e., originality and quality) of each idea. Second, this study identified latent profiles of students’ cognitive strategy use, and their relationship with creativity. Using a novel process-oriented theoretical framework and a combination of deductive and inductive analyses, six cognitive strategies were identified: repeat, unmediated, experiential, conceptual combination, semantic, and assumption reversal. A laboratory-based observational study involving 146 undergraduate students showed that constructive cognitive strategies (conceptual combination and semantic) were more frequently associated with highly original ideas than active cognitive strategies (unmediated and experiential), whereas no differences were found for idea quality. Furthermore, latent profile analysis identified four distinct profiles of human–AI collaboration: Largely Independent Thinkers, AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers. Although the profiles did not differ in their average originality, they differed significantly in their average quality. Students classified as AI-Constructive Combiners, AI-Balanced Thinkers, and AI-Reliant Reproducers produced ideas of higher quality than the Largely Independent Thinkers. These findings demonstrate that the way students cognitively engage with GenAI shapes their creativity and provide insights for fostering effective human–AI collaboration in higher education.

articles.title: Packaging Psychological Theory: A New Standard for Reusable Computational Models
articles.authors: Kyra Evers; Lourens Waldorp; Eiko I Fried; Fred Hasselman; Denny Borsboom
articles.abstract: Psychological theories are increasingly expressed as computational models to improve their rigour, robustness, and testability. Yet in the absence of shared standards for distributing such models, researchers often rely on idiosyncratic code formats. This creates large heterogeneity in the accessibility, quality, and intelligibility of models, making implementations difficult to reproduce, interpret, or extend. As a consequence, computational models are rarely reused, creating a vast space of isolated models with little effort towards theoretical integration. To address this challenge, we propose a new standard: computational models representing psychological theory should be distributed as software packages (e.g., in R, Python, or Julia). Packaged models should be openly available and licensed for reuse, documented and tested, checked by automated workflows, and preserved with a persistent identifier. Unlike static code archives, packages are tools made for users, with a familiar and engaging interface. Their format accommodates different programming languages, modelling frameworks, and stages of model development, giving authors substantial flexibility in how models are formalized and implemented. We illustrate the packaging standard with affectOU, an example R package implementing a psychological theory of affect dynamics. Our proposed standard draws on established infrastructure and best practices from software engineering to improve model quality and reproducibility. Adopting this standard would lower the cost of verifying and reusing computational models for authors, reviewers, and readers alike. In our view, improving model reusability is not optional but essential for cumulative progress in psychological theory.

articles.title: From Epic to Applied Psychology: A Conceptual Mapping of Sanskrit Psychological Constructs and Their Contemporary Relevance
articles.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles.abstract: This conceptual paper examines whether four Sanskrit epic constructs hold structural resonance with four established areas of psychological science. It responds to a growing interest in integrating Indian Knowledge Systems with psychological theory, extending that integration into underexplored epic material. Sanskrit's own literary and grammatical heritage has long been recognised in linguistics and aesthetics; this paper asks whether its psychological vocabulary deserves comparable recognition. Following a conceptual-article design (Theory Synthesis), the paper pairs dharma saṅkaṭa with moral cognition, tapas-nirvṛtti with self-regulation, rasa with affective science, and karma yoga with motivation theory. Four criteria—definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity—guided construct selection. Constructs were drawn from named episodes in the Mahābhārata, Kumārasambhava, and Buddhacarita, rather than from Sanskrit thought treated generally. Each pairing shows meaningful structural alignment without collapsing into a single unifying model. Applied implications extend to education, therapy, policy, and Gen-Z digital burnout, illustrating the pairings' contemporary relevance. Each pairing was illustrated through a textual episode and a contemporary vignette, grounding abstract resonance in concrete cases. The paper offers four testable propositions for future empirical validation. It also proposes a shared vocabulary bridging Sanskrit psychological thought and contemporary science, without claiming either tradition anticipated or exhausts the other.

articles.title: Moral Concern for AI in an Economic Game
articles.authors: Carter Allen; Joshua Lewis; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: How will people morally regard increasingly human-like artificial intelligence systems? We introduce the AI Harm Game, a novel paradigm examining whether people will harm AI for personal gain. In our study, 498 U.S. participants interacted with GPT-4o in a three-round economic game. In each round, participants chose whether to harm the AI for a small monetary bonus (causing it to vividly simulate suffering) or refrain from harming it (eliciting gratitude). Although participants were overwhelmingly skeptical that current AIs can suffer, their decisions and reasoning about whether to harm the AI varied considerably. Participants harmed the AI in 1.4 out of 3 rounds on average. Women and older participants were more reluctant to harm the AI, while participants higher on measures of selfishness and psychopathy were more willing. These findings reveal that even without attributing consciousness to them, many people hesitate to harm responsive AIs, suggesting people’s moral impulses may generalize to future human–AI relationships.

articles.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles.title: Does internalized homonegativity lower sexual satisfaction? A longitudinal assessment among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) in Canada's three largest cities
articles.authors: Sarah Meora Kowall; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Aki Gormezano; Jérémy Lelièvre; Darell H.S. Tan; Daniel Grace; Trevor Adam Hart
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Internalized homonegativity is associated with lower sexual satisfaction among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Though internalized homonegativity is commonly seen as an antecedent to lower sexual satisfaction, existing research tends to be cross-sectional, limiting our ability to make causal inferences. This has important implications for GBM sexual health and clinical interventions. The goal of this study is to examine the longitudinal associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction.

Methods: We analyzed data from a longitudinal study of GBM in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, Canada (N = 1307). Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), we analyzed data from baseline up to two years of follow-up to model the within-person changes in internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction. The RI-CLPM allowed us to account for the stable differences between individuals that may inflate correlations, thus allowing for a stronger estimate of within-person variation over time.

Results: There were no cross-lagged associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction, but there were significant random-intercept associations such that participants who scored higher on internalized homonegativity tended to score lower on sexual satisfaction.

Conclusion: Our findings suggest that cross-sectional associations in past research  are likely due to stable between-person differences and that internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction may be independent processes. From a clinical perspective, internalized homonegativity may be useful in identifying potential issues with sexual (dis)satisfaction, but reducing internalized homonegativity may not be sufficient in alleviating these challenges.

articles.title: “A Freeing of My Mind”: Narrative Accounts of Perinatal Mental Health in the Context of   Rx Kids, a Prenatal and Infant Unconditional Cash Transfer Program
articles.authors: Caroline Doenmez; Crystal L. Cederna; Mona Hanna
articles.abstract:
Background: In 2024, a new program called Rx Kids began providing unconditional cash transfers to all expectant mothers and infants in Flint, Michigan. Through a lump sum payment provided mid-pregnancy and monthly payments for up to a year after birth, the place-based maternal and infant health program is aimed at providing economic stability to improve the health, hope, and happiness of mothers and newborns.  

Objective: This study examined how mothers who had received Rx Kids cash transfers discussed perceived impacts on their perinatal mental health while participating in the program.  

Design: Qualitative.  

Methods: Thematic analysis was used to analyze interviews conducted between July and October 2025 with 46 mothers from Flint, Michigan, who participated in the Rx Kids program. Conceptual frameworks from medical anthropology and psychology were utilized to interpret their narratives.  

Results: Three dominant themes emerged pertaining to mothers’ experiences of perinatal mental health in the context of receiving Rx Kids cash transfers: 1) financial relief and perinatal well-being; 2) postpartum time affluence; and 3) program communication as a form of care.  

Conclusion: For mothers in Flint, Michigan, financial concerns play a central role in their narratives of their perinatal mental health struggles with stress and postpartum depression. Analyzing their descriptions of perceived shifts, adaptions and relief associated with their participation in Rx Kids, we find that the program was often depicted as equally impactful in terms of improving mothers’ mental health as it was in easing financial pressures.

articles.title: The beliefs at the heart of multilingual family language policies: A corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism
articles.authors: Ruth Kircher; Melanie Brouillard; Alexa Ahooja; Erin Quirk; Susan Ballinger; Linda Polka; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: This study focuses on parental language beliefs, which we approach from an attitudes perspective. Language attitudes are at the heart of multilingual family language policies because they shape parents’ language practices and language management – and thereby, ultimately, children’s multilingual development. Based on French and English corpora (over 30,000 words in total) comprising 742 Quebec-based parents’ responses to an open-ended survey question, we present a corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism. We analyse frequencies and collocations to attest statistically significant patterns, and we examine concordance lines and longer text segments to establish meaning in context. Our findings confirm the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, providing new insights into the nature of the three previously-established dimensions – status, solidarity, and cognitive development – as well as revealing a potential fourth dimension: personality development. The study thus makes a contribution to the family language policy framework and to language attitude theory more generally. Moreover, the findings show systematic differences between parents transmitting multiple societal languages versus parents transmitting heritage languages alongside one/more societal languages. The study thus also makes a practical contribution by facilitating the development of tailored support measures for different types of multilingual families.

articles.title: Continuous-Time Subgrouping of Heterogeneous Time-Series
articles.authors: Jonathan JaeHong Park; Nathan Xin Mills; Harriette Riese; Omid V. Ebrahimi
articles.abstract: The clinical and behavioral sciences have increasingly focused on the treatment and modeling of individuals as complex, dynamical systems. This rise in idiographic theories and applications has led to concerns regarding the generalizability of results based on person-specific analyses. Several methodological techniques have been developed to address these concerns via the identification of subgroups. Many of these approaches are based in the discrete-time framework and inherit the limitations of that framework such as sensitivity to sampling rates. As such, clustering methods based on discrete-time dynamic parameters may suffer from what we refer to as, “illusory homogeneity”. We present a subgrouping extension to continuous-time Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation (cts-gimme) framework which enables researchers to identify homogeneous subgroups of individuals in multivariate time-series. Simulation results indicated that cts-gimme maintained consistent classification of individuals across sampling rates, whereas the discrete-time methods were comparatively more dependent on sampling intervals.

articles.title: Playing for fun, playing to escape: Gaming motives and problematic video game use in a French sample aged 6 to 45 years
articles.authors: Chloe Nguyen; Quentin Hallez
articles.abstract: Data on the prevalence of problematic gaming in France are scarce, and few studies have compared gaming behavior, gaming motives, and their correlates across developmental periods with identical instruments. We surveyed 676 French participants aged 6 to 45 years (52.4% male), spanning childhood (6–14 years; parent-reported), adolescence (15–17), young adulthood (18–25), and adulthood (26–45), using the Game Addiction Scale (GAS-7), the Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ), the WHO-5 Well-Being Index, and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-15). Overall, 79.6% of participants played video games. Problematic gaming (monothetic GAS criterion) characterized 4.8% of gamers, with no significant differences across age groups and rates three times higher in males than in females. Although symptom levels were similar across age groups, motive profiles were not: recreation dominated at every age, whereas coping and escape motives were rare in childhood and markedly higher from adolescence onward. In hierarchical regressions, escape and competition motives and gaming frequency were the strongest unique correlates of problematic use, statistically attenuating the bivariate contributions of gender, impulsivity, well-being, and gaming time. Motive–symptom associations were invariant across age groups, whereas the association between gaming time and symptoms was stronger in older age groups. These cross-sectional findings suggest that motivational assessment may be more informative than screen-time metrics for the prevention and screening of problematic gaming.

articles.title: Getting Closer or Stepping Back? Personal Space Adjustments Following Facial Emotion Imitation and Observation
articles.authors: Ivan Patané; Clément Desoche; ALESSANDRO FARNE; Fadila Hadj-Bouziane
articles.abstract: Regulating personal space (PS) is essential for navigating social interactions. Although emotional cues are known to influence PS, the mechanisms underlying this modulation remain poorly understood. The present study investigated whether active facial emotion imitation is followed by changes in PS regulation and whether these changes differ from those observed following passive emotion observation. Participants completed a Virtual Reality Stop-Distance task to assess their preferred interpersonal distances from angry, happy, and neutral virtual agents, before and after an imitation session, during which they actively imitated angry or happy facial expressions. Following emotion imitation, participants exhibited a bidirectional modulation of PS: they increased their distance from angry virtual agents and decreased it from happy virtual agents, while no changes were observed for neutral agents. These findings suggest that active facial imitation enhances sensitivity to emotional signals and adaptively modulates interpersonal distance. Eye-tracking analyses revealed no significant changes in gaze behavior between pre- and post-imitation sessions, indicating that the reported effects were not driven by differences in overt visual attention. In a second experiment using a similar pre-post design, a new group of participants passively observed the same emotional expressions without imitating them. Results showed that, after emotion observation, angry virtual agents elicited an increased interpersonal distance, whereas no changes in distance from either the happy or neutral virtual agents were observed. Together, these results indicate that defensive distancing from others’ angry expressions followed both active imitation and passive observation, whereas the approach-related reduction in distance in response to happy expressions was evident after active imitation only. These findings highlight the contribution of emotional-cue exposure to personal space regulation in social contexts and provide further evidence that emotional experience can dynamically shape interpersonal behavior.

articles.title: Lines We Cross: Identity Complexity at the Boundary Between Activism and Radicalism
articles.authors: Michelle Blaya-Burgo
articles.abstract: Violent radicalization and politically motivated violence pose significant threats to global peace, security, and social cohesion. These problems are costly, and reactive approaches have not effectively reduced their incidence. Because conflict is inevitable, prevention efforts should take precedence. This paper examines social identity complexity as a potential buffer against violent radicalization, proposing that complex identity structures – perceptions of having multiple, distinct ingroup memberships – may reduce susceptibility by preventing individuals from fixating on a single identity and pushing it to extremes. Two studies tested this idea. Study 1 (N = 226) used a 2×2 design manipulating identity complexity (simple vs. complex) and self-uncertainty (low vs. high). Results showed that simple identity structures increased radicalism intentions, resulting in a greater relative preference for activism among those with complex identities. Study 2 (N = 240) examined political identity and natural levels of identity-uncertainty. Results showed that higher uncertainty predicted more radicalism. Further, when political identity was highly salient, uncertainty increased intentions to engage in radicalism. Across studies, most participants favored activism over radicalism; however, the findings suggest that uncertainty can push intentions toward more extreme forms of action, while access to multiple identities may help protect against fixation on a single identity.

articles.title: Unpacking cognitive variability: Dynamic systems modeling to understand daily cognitive change in healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
articles.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Joshua James Jackson
articles.abstract: It is increasingly accepted that single scores are insufficient to fully capture the complexities of cognition as it relates to daily life. Many studies now employ repeated cognitive assessments to measure variability in scores across the testing sessions. Exploration of additional characteristics of participant’s time series may provide more explanatory power in understanding cognitive health in aging and early neurodegenerative disease. We administered a standard attention test daily for 3 weeks to healthy younger adults, healthy older adults and participants diagnosed with cognitive impairment. Participants self-rated the frequency of their cognitive failures in daily life. We used an established cognitive model to decompose participant scores into two latent parameters, mean inputs and “dissipation” which reflects the speed with which one returns to baseline performance after a deviation in scores. More traditional summary statistics, including mean performance and variability, were also calculated. Linear regression was used to compare group differences on each outcome and their association with real-world cognitive failures. Results indicate that variability in scores followed a U-shaped pattern across groups. Variability changes in cognitive impairment were due exclusively to changes in the dissipation parameter and this parameter was uniquely related to self-rated cognitive failures. Our findings indicate dissipation may reflect high levels of cognitive reserve, which protects against the manifestation of functional symptoms in daily life. More generally, our results underscore the importance of using repeated cognitive assessments in studies of healthy and pathological aging, as traditional measures of performance did not evince relationships with cognitive failures.

articles.title: A questionnaire survey on context-dependent requirements for the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence and humans
articles.authors: Satoshi Nishida
articles.abstract: Trustworthiness has become an important focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research. Although trustworthiness is a multifaceted concept and its requirements may depend on the context in which AI is used, little is known about how the public perceives these requirements. To address this issue, we conducted a questionnaire survey with nonexpert participants to examine the requirements that the public considers important for trustworthy AI and how their perceived value differs between social and nonsocial contexts. We further compared these context-dependent patterns with those observed for human trustworthiness. Our findings showed that, across social and nonsocial contexts, confidentiality and privacy protection were among the most important requirements for AI trustworthiness whereas the relative importance of other requirements depended on the context. In nonsocial contexts, transparency and interpretability of decision-making were particularly important whereas in social contexts, the ability to collaborate and communicate and a positive public image and attractive appearance were predominantly significant. Although similar context-dependent patterns were observed for human trustworthiness, findings consistently highlighted the ability to collaborate and communicate as a requirement for trusting humans, regardless of context, in contrast to AI trustworthiness. These findings provide insights into the public’s perception of trustworthy AI and highlight the importance of considering the context in which AI is used when examining AI trustworthiness requirements.

articles.title: Amotivated Solitude: Naming the Space Between Vairagya and Escapism
articles.authors: Pooja Tyagi; Baljeet Kaur
articles.abstract: Recent global data indicate that roughly one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, prompting the World Health Organization to name social disconnection a public health priority. Yet not everyone who prefers solitude over social engagement is lonely, distressed, or withdrawing from life. A growing body of solitude research documents this distinction, but the specific combination addressed here, a preference for solitude that is neither reactively avoidant nor autonomously growth-seeking, remains unnamed. This preference is neither the growth-oriented non-attachment described by the Indian philosophical concept of Vairagya, nor the reactive, affect-driven retreat captured by passive escapism, nor the impairment associated with loneliness or clinical depression, nor the positively-valenced enjoyment described by affinity for aloneness. This paper proposes Amotivated Solitude (Preference) to name this gap: a dispositional or situational preference for solitude that is low in both autonomous, growth-seeking motivation and reactive, anxiety-driven avoidance. Drawing on self-determination theory's amotivation continuum, the solitude-motivation literature, and the developmental construct of unsociability, this paper differentiates the proposed construct from eight neighbouring constructs, addresses the risk of construct proliferation (the jingle-jangle problem) directly, and presents a conceptual map locating the construct along a volition-outcome spectrum. It outlines a research program for construct validation, including qualitative grounding, item development, and psychometric testing against existing non-attachment measures, and closes with limitations and open questions for discussion regarding naming, boundary conditions, and trait versus state framing.

articles.title: An Experience-Sampling Study of Daily Affect and Global Life Satisfaction in the United States and Japan
articles.authors: Hiroki Hirano
articles.abstract: Evidence for cultural differences in affect–life satisfaction associations has largely come from retrospective measures, and whether these variations also emerge when emotional experiences are captured in daily life remains less clear. Therefore, the present study analyzed experience-sampling data collected over a two-week period to examine associations of momentary positive and negative affect with global life satisfaction among U.S. and Japanese adults. In both groups, higher positive affect and lower negative affect were each uniquely associated with greater life satisfaction. The primary analysis also indicated a stronger relationship between positive affect and life satisfaction among Japanese than U.S. participants, although this cultural contrast was not consistently statistically significant across sensitivity analyses. Meanwhile, the strength of the link between negative affect and life satisfaction did not differ significantly between the two groups. Considered alongside prior research using retrospective reports, the current findings highlight the importance of both cultural context and assessment methods in understanding the emotional correlates of life satisfaction.

articles.title: Grounding meaning in social and emotional experience: Challenges and opportunities
articles.authors: Pablo Solana
articles.abstract: Within the broader debate on how the mind and brain represent meaning, multiple representation theories have positioned social and emotional experience, along with their underlying neural systems, as key sources for concept grounding. In this article, I review the current evidence for this proposal and discuss several conceptual and methodological challenges, including the limited capacity of behavioral evidence to support this view, the difficulties associated with interpreting neuroimaging findings, the need for stronger causal evidence, and the importance of adopting open science practices. I argue that these limitations converge on a common concern: in their current form, many findings taken to support multiple representation theories of socio-affective grounding do not provide sufficiently diagnostic evidence to empirically adjudicate between them and competing accounts of semantic representation. In response, I outline a set of methodological recommendations and underexplored ideas that may help refine the theoretical framework, generate more decisive tests, and guide future research.

articles.title: Revisiting Cross-Modal Matching in the Light of Luce’s Global Psychophysical Theory
articles.authors: Katharina Naumann; Jürgen Heller
articles.abstract: This study presents a replication of the classical cross-modal matching experiment by J. C. Stevens and Marks (1965, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 54, 407-411), which examined loudness-to-brightness and brightness-to-loudness mappings.  We extend prior work by complementing traditional group-level analysis with an individual-level examination and by applying the theory of global psychophysics with internal references. This mathematical framework formalizes the underlying mechanisms of cross-modal matching behavior. In matching tasks, the well-documented phenomenon termed the regression effect emerges, wherein the adjusted stimuli gravitate toward mid-level intensities. To model this effect, we implement a novel Bayesian estimation of the global psychophysical model for cross-modal matching. In a sample of seven subjects, including many repetitions at the subject level, the regression effect is observed at both the aggregated and individual levels. The model effectively captures the prevalent nonlinearity in individual matching curves. We discuss the theoretical and methodological implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

articles.title: Adaptive search promotes asymmetrical learning
articles.authors: Samuel David Jones; Paul Rauwolf
articles.abstract: Recent theoretical work has argued that learning trajectories are shaped by adaptive search and satisficing. The central idea of this work is that the value of an information source (i.e., its utility or valence) modulates engagement, sampling density, and encoding fidelity, providing a behavioural pathway to variation in learning outcomes. The current manuscript reports the first explicit empirical test of this idea in adults using a modified version of a multi-step decision-making paradigm known as 'Mouselab'. Across two experiments and six sub-tasks, N=101 participants searched a decision tree at a cost until settling on and executing a high-value policy. While Experiment 1 involved a non-symbolic decision space, Experiment 2 incorporated symbolic cues that allowed us to determine the extent to which associative learning is sensitive to underlying value structure. We found that value-sensitive adaptive search promoted rank-dependent learning asymmetries at test – estimates for the value of the best symbol were near veridical, while those for low-value symbols were at chance. In addition, we found that (i) informative symbolic cues shifted search from balanced exploration (breadth ≈ depth) towards depth-first exploitation; (ii) cue-guided search developed rapidly, with high-value symbol exploitation emerging within a handful of trials; (iii) search evidenced a win-stay tendency and was sensitive to cue valence, with individuals quickly pruning negatively valued branches; (iv) raising cost constrained search volume but preserved its depth-first, cue-sensitive character; and (v) observed individual differences in search behaviour were not predicted by common measures of cognitive function. These results provide new insight into how adaptive search and satisficing shape learning, supporting an emerging theory of the behavioural origins of individual differences in human development.

articles.title: Effects of task-switch proportion and strategy instructions on cognitive stability and flexibility
articles.authors: Lara Sophie Knaup; Marcus Möschl; John Dylan Haynes; Marie Therese Bartossek; Thomas Goschke
articles.abstract: To meet the challenges of daily life, we must continuously adapt to optimize the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility depending on the current task demands. The control dilemma theory posits that cognitive stability and flexibility are polar opposites on the same dimension incurring opposing costs and benefits, resulting in a trade-off. Accordingly, a shift towards flexibility (i.e., reducing costs of task-switching) incurs costs in stability (i.e., increasing interference costs), and vice versa. Here, we manipulated the list-wide proportion of task-switches between a flexibility (75% task-repeats) and a stability (25% task-switches) condition. We interspersed coveted trial sequences with balanced task transitions between strongly biased sequences while retaining the list-wide 75:25 ratios. Additionally, we asked participants to adapt to the prevalent transition type by behaving more flexible or stable. We hypothesized that switch costs would be reduced within the flexibility condition, that simultaneously reduced interference in the stability condition would be indicative of a trade-off, and that both control adaptations would persist within the balanced trial sequences. In a within-subjects design, participants (N = 96) completed two online sessions of a classic cued task-switching paradigm. While we did not observe the hypothesized trade-off in either of the two sequence types, the level of flexibility was adapted within the biased sequences, but this effect decayed within the balanced sequences. Taken together, these results highlight that individuals are able to adapt cognitive control modes supporting cognitive flexibility remarkably fast in response to dynamic changes in the likelihood of local trial transitions.

articles.title: Relationship Microcultures Theory
articles.authors: Maya Rossignac-Milon; Emma S Miller; Lydia Emery; Joshua Conrad Jackson; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Just as groups of people form large-scale macro-cultures, close relationship partners construct their own microculture. Dyads invent their own language (the word “muddles” for homemade ceramics), stories (rescuing their cat), rituals (weekly backgammon), morality (conflicts require mutual apologies), identity (activists), and sense of reality (belief in UFOs). We contend that the emergence, development, and maintenance of this co-created microculture predicts key relational and personal outcomes. We introduce Relationship Microcultures Theory (RMT), which complements prevailing relationship theories by examining how particular words and behaviors are interpreted within the history of the specific relationship in which they acquired idiosyncratic meaning, shaping in turn the well-being of the relationship and the individuals involved. In our Microcultural Unit Model, we describe a meta-theory for understanding how particular dyadic interactions become microcultural units (e.g., inside jokes) by acquiring mutual, idiosyncratic, and referential meaning. In our Aggregate Microculture Model, we advance a theory of how more extensive microcultures—those comprising more units, used more frequently, and spanning more life domains—contribute to relational outcomes (e.g., relationship satisfaction and longevity) and personal outcomes (e.g., meaning in life and self-regulatory success). We also theorize that microcultural extensiveness can undermine relational and personal outcomes when mutuality, idiosyncrasy, and referentiality are low. By examining the dyad as a culture in miniature, RMT opens novel research directions for relationship science.

articles.title: Quantifying the relative associations of time of social media use and addictive social media use with emotional distress among U.S. adults
articles.authors: Hyosin Kim; Jakub Helvich; Giselle Lee; Brian Primack
articles.abstract: Both time of social media use (TSMU) and addictive social media use (ASMU) have been associated with depression and anxiety. However, their relative associations with emotional distress remain unclear, and research involving middle-aged and older adults has been limited. We examined associations of TSMU and ASMU with depression and anxiety in a probability-based nationally-representative sample of 1512 U.S. adults aged 30–70 years. Depression and anxiety were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, respectively. TSMU and ASMU, assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, were both operationalized in quartiles to facilitate direct comparison. In separate weighted logistic regression models, both TSMU and ASMU were associated with depression and anxiety. However, when TSMU and ASMU were included in the same models, associations between TSMU and both depression and anxiety became non-significant, whereas associations between ASMU and both outcomes remained strong (p<0.001 for both). Compared with participants in the lowest quartile of ASMU, those in the highest quartile had between 4 and 5 times the odds for depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 4.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.20–7.62), and anxiety (AOR, 4.59; 95% CI, 2.76–7.63), even after adjusting for TSMU. These findings suggest that ASMU may be more strongly associated with depression and anxiety than overall amount of social media use among U.S. adults.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: The three biggest obstacles to solving motivated behavior, and how to overcome them
articles.authors: Amitai Shenhav
articles.abstract: Humans and other animals have a wide repertoire of actions they can engage in at any given moment, ranging from moving their limbs to generating utterances to controlling the flow of information from perception to action. What motivates them to engage some of these actions and not others at any given moment? To answer this question, motivation scientists have historically leveraged three kinds of explanatory variables: goals (what directs action), value (what determines a good or bad action), and affect (what it feels like if an action is or isn’t taken). I will argue that each of these variables faces significant challenges in explaining motivated behavior: Goals can explain how actions are directed, but not what directs goals; value can be assigned to an action, but it is a mystery how these values are assigned and how they are shaped by both “cold” and “hot” systems; and affect can explain what actions will make you feel best, but under most definitions affect is neither specific nor reliable enough to guide action selection. My Affective Gradient Hypothesis (AGH) proposes a way out of this entanglement, by re-centering motivation on two sets of processes: prediction and optimization. AGH suggests that motivated behavior arises from the continual representation of potential future states and their affective value, and the dynamic adjustment of available actions and control states to achieve states that are anticipated to be most positive and/or least negative. This account revises traditional definitions of goals, value, and affect to overcome existing obstacles and to provide a complete, coherent, empirically grounded, and generalizable account of what drives motivated behavior.

articles.title: From Unstructured Text to Causal Inference: Addressing Proxy Measurement Error and Omitted Variable Bias
articles.authors: Soojin Park; Luke Rabelhofer; Su Yeon Kim; Chioun Lee
articles.abstract: Unstructured text offers a rich source of nuanced information that is often difficult to capture with structured survey measures. However, Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools result in labels prone to measurement error, which can cause significant bias and invalid statistical inference. Although several studies have proposed methods to address measurement error in text-extracted measures, these solutions often rely on the ``no omitted confounders'' assumption, which is rarely met in observational settings. Addressing measurement error in isolation from omitted variable bias is often insufficient for valid causal conclusions. Therefore, this study aims to provide a rigorous and credible foundation for drawing causal conclusions from unstructured text in observational settings. To do this, we derive nonparametric and parametric bias formulas for cases in which 1) we ignore both omitted confounders and measurement error and 2) we correct measurement error in a treatment proxy while ignoring omitted confounders. Based on these bias formulas, we develop a framework for estimating Average Treatment Effects using a text-derived treatment that addresses the dual challenges of measurement error and omitted confounders. We illustrate our proposed methods using unstructured data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study to examine the effect of social interaction on cardiovascular health.

articles.title: Nonsuicidal self-injury and approach behavior toward aversive images:  A MouseView.js study
articles.authors: Sarina Rain; Lily Wanlu Martin; Edwin S. Dalmaijer; Thomas Armstrong; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is associated with altered responses to self-injury-related cues. However, extant behavioral measures do not capture intentional engagement with stimuli, which may be most clinically relevant to understanding persistent NSSI. 

Methods: We created a novel task in MouseView.js to measure voluntary engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli using cursor movements. Young adults (N=143) with self-injurious thoughts and/or behaviors histories completed the task and questionnaires assessing NSSI and suicidal ideation (SI) at baseline and 2-, 4- and 6-month follow-ups.

Results: More frequent NSSI and greater SI severity were associated with increased engagement with suicide images (i.e., staged suicide attempts), but not general gore images, across the 10-second viewing period. Greater average engagement with both image types was associated with the presence (versus absence) of past-month NSSI. Greater baseline engagement with both image types prospectively predicted NSSI frequency over follow-ups; however, effects were non-significant when controlling for baseline symptoms.

Conclusion: We provide preliminary evidence that engagement with NSSI-relevant stimuli – measured using cursor movements – may be a concurrent behavioral correlate of NSSI. Effects were most consistent for images depicting self-injury, compared to general gore, suggesting that individuals with NSSI may be especially prone to engaging with content depicting intentional self-directed harm.

articles.title: Maternal Emotional Experiences During Everyday Infant Soothing: Within- and Between-Person Predictors from an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Sarvenaz Oloomi; Alexis Hernandez; Alexa Monachino; Irene Tung; Lauren C Shuffrey; Santiago Morales
articles.abstract: Infant crying and mothers’ efforts to soothe their infants are highly emotional experiences that shape parent–infant co-regulation and bonding. Despite the importance of this process, relatively little research has examined how mothers feel when they soothe their infants, especially with real-time, ecologically-relevant measures. In this study, we collected ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a geographically representative sample between September 2022 and September 2025 for up to 14 days to capture mothers’ (N = 250; Mage = 33.2 years, range = 19–45, 51.5% Hispanic/Latinx) emotional experiences during soothing interactions with their infants (Mage = 9.4 months, range = 3–23 months; 52.8% female; 57% Hispanic/Latinx). Mothers also completed questionnaires about their distress (anxiety, depression, and stress) symptoms and their infant’s temperamental negative affectivity. Within-person analyses revealed that maternal positive affect decreased and negative affect increased as soothing became longer and more difficult. Between-person analyses indicated that higher infant negative affectivity and greater maternal distress were associated with mothers reporting more negative emotions while soothing, whereas more positive maternal emotions were related to less maternal distress. Results were present while accounting for mothers’ mood while completing the survey, soothing difficulty and duration, infant age and sex, and socioeconomic factors. These findings highlight that soothing can be a particularly challenging and emotional experience for mothers high in distress symptoms and those with infants high in temperamental negative affectivity, pointing to the need for targeted interventions within this population that support maternal emotion regulation and parent-infant interaction quality.

articles.title: The Architecture of Academic Safety: Supervisory Communication, the Impostor Phenomenon, and Doctoral Psychological Well-Being—A Mixed-Methods Study"
articles.authors: Varsha singh; Rajnesh meena; Saloni vishwakarma
articles.abstract:
NOTICE: This manuscript is currently under peer review at a journal. This version is the Author's Original Manuscript (AOM) and has not yet undergone formal peer review.

The doctoral journey increases risks for poor psychological well-being and the impostor phenomenon. This mixed-methods study examined how supervisor communication style influences these experiences among PhD scholars. Quantitative data were gathered via an online survey from 90 scholars, alongside qualitative interview data from 20 participants. Quantitative results indicated that scholars generally perceived their supervisors’ communication positively (M = 3.78, SD = 0.42), reported moderate levels of the impostor phenomenon (M = 2.42, SD = 0.99), and demonstrated relatively high psychological well-being (M = 4.26, SD = 0.70). Supervisor communication style was not significantly related to the impostor phenomenon (r = .074, p = .484) but showed a significant positive relationship with psychological well-being (r = .206, p = .049; R² = .043). The impostor phenomenon was negatively, but not significantly, related to well-being (r = -.196, p = .061). Crucially, however, qualitative findings explained this disconnect by revealing that specific, nuanced communication types heavily dictate these experiences. Qualitative findings revealed that instructive clarity, affective support, autonomy, scholarly inclusion, academic recognition, and constructive feedback characterized positive communication, whereas structural ambiguity, inconsistent feedback, intellectual exclusion, systematic invalidation and controlling behaviours induced stress and experienced high imposter phenomenon

articles.title: Navigating consumer uncertainty: Curiosity and individual differences in exploratory consumer behavior
articles.authors: Collin Kather; David M. Lydon-Staley
articles.abstract: Consumers differ not only in whether they explore marketplaces, but also in how they explore them. We examined whether multidimensional curiosity helps explain two forms of exploratory consumer behavior: exploratory acquisition of products and exploratory information seeking. Across two independent samples of adults (Study 1, N=461; Study 2, N=337), participants completed measures of six curiosity dimensions and exploratory consumer behavior. Stress tolerance was uniquely associated with greater exploratory acquisition in both studies after accounting for the other curiosity dimensions. Covert social curiosity was uniquely associated with greater exploratory information seeking in both studies. Associations between thrill seeking and acquisition and between overt social curiosity and information seeking emerged in Study 1 but did not replicate in Study 2. Joyous exploration and deprivation sensitivity showed bivariate associations with exploratory behavior but did not explain unique variance consistently. These findings indicate that a multidimensional curiosity framework provides a more differentiated account of the psychological heterogeneity underlying how consumers navigate uncertain marketplaces.

articles.title: Context-specific adaptation of cognitive processing in changing virtual environments
articles.authors: Ulrike Senftleben; Daniel Zeidler; Stefan Scherbaum; Matthew McGinity; Caroline Surrey
articles.abstract: Human cognition is sensitive to context cues, as indicated by the context-specific proportion congruency (CSPC) effect. This effect demonstrates that individuals implicitly adapt their cognitive processing to contextual cues that predict the likelihood of conflict. However, CSPC paradigms typically rely on simple, two-dimensional context cues, raising questions about their validity for complex, real-life environments. In this preregistered study, we examined whether CSPC effects emerge in three-dimensional, naturalistic contexts delivered via virtual reality (VR). We presented a numerical Stroop task in two virtual environments—a forest and an office—alternating on a trial-by-trial basis. Unbeknownst to participants, each environment was paired with either a high (80%; mostly congruent/MC context) or low (20%; mostly incongruent/MI context) proportion of incongruent trials (counter-balanced). Our results show the typical CSPC effect: reduced response time differences between incongruent and congruent trials in the MI environment relative to the MC environment. This finding indicates that context-dependent adjustments of cognitive processing extend to complex, semantically meaningful virtual environments. This supports the ecological validity of CSPC learning and highlights the importance of context cues in real-life cognitive processing. Further, our study highlights how VR opens up new avenues for studying context-dependent cognition beyond conventional laboratory stimuli.

articles.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles.title: Made in the Image of the Creator? AI Use in Creative Work Reduces Authenticity, Love and Other Psychological Benefits
articles.authors: Jessica Carson; Paul H.P. Hanel; Wijnand A. P. van Tilburg
articles.abstract: Across psychological, philosophical, and theological traditions, creations have been understood as being “made in the image of their creator”—they reflect the person who made them. The rise of generative artificial intelligence, however, has blurred the throughline between creator and creation. Across three experiments (one pre-registered, U.S. and U.K. samples; N = 651), we examined differences in creator outcomes associated with AI-assisted versus human-only creative work. Compared with human-only work, AI-assisted work was associated with significantly lower self- and identity-relevant indicators, including authenticity, self-creation connection, positive affect, and intrinsic motivation, and with higher levels of the “existential ick” emotions of disgust, guilt, and shame. Additionally, we found that the authenticity gap was statistically mediated by the creators’ perception that their AI-assisted work contains less of their love, above and beyond differences in perceived effort, uniqueness, quality, and expensiveness. We also ruled out effort justification as an alternative explanation. Together, these findings suggest that AI reshapes not only how creative work is produced, but also the extent to which creators experience their work as an authentic expression and extension of themselves.

articles.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health Dynamics in Daily Life
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: Experiences of selflessness and happiness are interconnected in everyday life. Both between-person and within-person variations in selflessness are associated with higher and more stable happiness. However, little is known about the role of selflessness in shaping negative mental health at the experiential level. Moreover, self-centeredness, the second regulatory process proposed by the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), has received little empirical attention. This experience sampling study addresses these gaps by examining the dynamic effects of selflessness and self-centeredness, between and within individuals. These effects were assessed on positive and negative mental health, as well as on relationship quality with others and nature. Results reveal distinct yet complementary roles for selflessness and self-centeredness: selflessness fosters and stabilizes mental health, self-centeredness undermines it and introduces greater variability. These findings offer insights into the psychological mechanisms underlying complete mental health and illuminate how these processes shape our connection with the social and natural environment.

articles.title: Differential Effects of Self-centeredness and Selflessness: A Six-Month Longitudinal Study Across Mental, Relational, and Ecological Domains
articles.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles.abstract: The Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM) posits two complementary modes of self-based psychological functioning, selflessness and self-centeredness, relevant across multiple subfields of psychology. Shaped by developmental, social and cultural influences, selflessness and self-centeredness differentially forecast multiple variables from individual mental health to ecological concerns and behaviors. Addressing the largely correlational nature of prior evidence on the model, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal study over six months (N = 316) to test the middle-term prospective effects of selflessness and self-centeredness on mental health, relationship quality, and ecological orientation. Controlling for autoregressive stability and within-wave covariation, cross-lagged panel models indicated that selflessness prospectively predicted higher positive mental health and lower negative mental health and ecoanxiety. By contrast, self-centeredness predicted lower positive mental health, relationship quality and relationship with nature, and higher negative mental health. Additional findings revealed the mutual inhibition between the two dispositions. These findings extend cross-sectional research on the SSHM by demonstrating medium-term prospective associations and by positioning selflessness and self-centeredness as transdisciplinary predictors of holistic forms of health spanning intrapersonal, interpersonal, and ecological domains.

articles.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles.title: Artificial Neutrality: Bias and Omission in Large Language Models’ Descriptions of Urban Wildlife
articles.authors: Sam Gowland; Lauren Scott; djt.vanderlinden@gmail.com; Shaun Lawson
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly prominent AI applications, but they remain vulnerable to bias rooted in their training data. Such bias matters in the context of animals, since LLM outputs can influence human attitudes and behaviours toward wildlife. To explore this, we conducted a word association experiment with human participants (N = 300) and with three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini). Each was asked to provide five keywords for species commonly viewed positively (hedgehogs), negatively (rats), and with mixed attitudes (foxes). Sentiment analysis showed that humans exhibited greater variability, generally reflecting expected
attitudes toward each species. LLMs, by contrast, did not reproduce these distributions. Their responses leaned toward neutral or ecological terms rather than emotive words, diverging from typical human conceptualisations.
Our findings suggest that while LLMs may reduce bias through neutralisation, they risk introducing new distortions, underscoring the need for careful, balanced application in wildlife-related contexts.

articles.title: Environmental and social context are associated with emotional states and their dynamics
articles.authors: Florencia Altschuler; Christophe Gauld; Enric Vilajosana; Cecilia González Campo; Pamela Chavarría-Elizondo; Víctor De la Peña-Arteaga; Asier Juaneda-Seguí; Ignacio Martínez-Zalacaín; VIktor Jirsa; Pierpaolo Sorrentino
articles.abstract: Emotional states fluctuate with everyday context, but contextual influences can operate at markedly different temporal scales and magnitudes. We examined the longitudinal effects of two naturalistic contextual exposures - daily weather (precipitation and temperature) and the COVID-19 lockdown-  on emotional states assessed using ecological momentary assessment (EMA) in a university-based cohort in Barcelona, Spain, comprising up to 25,724 observations from 156 participants. Lockdown analyses were restricted to the subset of participants with observations both during and outside the lockdown period (n=45). Participants completed daily smartphone-based assessments of happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, worry, and avoidance over six months. Within-participant fixed-effects models showed that greater precipitation was associated with lower happiness and higher anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance, whereas temperature showed no significant associations with any of these outcomes. In contrast, lockdown was associated with a broad shift toward lower happiness and higher negative emotional states and with greater day-to-day variability in happiness, anxiety, muscular tension, and avoidance. These findings illustrate how low-magnitude environmental variation and large-scale social disruption can be detected within the same real-world EMA framework, with the latter affecting both emotional states and short-term dynamics.

articles.title: Differential Effects of Task-Context and Stimulus-Category Changes on Recognition Memory: A Replication and Extension of Morse et al. (2023)
articles.authors: Raju Pooja; Pritha Ghosh; Vishnu Sreekumar
articles.abstract: Event segmentation is the process by which ongoing experience is organized into discrete events, with event boundaries marking transitions between successive events. Although contextual changes are thought to trigger event segmentation, different types of contextual change may vary in their effectiveness and their consequences for subsequent memory. In the present study, which is a replication of Morse et al. (2023), albeit with some methodological improvements, we examined whether stimulus-category shifts and task-context shifts produce differential consequences for recognition memory and mnemonic discrimination. Across three experiments using the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), event boundaries were instantiated by changes in image category (Experiment 1), encoding task (Experiment 2) or both simultaneously (Experiment 3). Task-context shifts produced reliable behavioral signatures of event segmentation, reflected by an increase in post-boundary encoding response times, and also led to impaired recognition memory for items encountered immediately after a boundary. In contrast, stimulus-category shifts alone produced neither time processing costs nor memory impairments. Critically, combining stimulus-category and task-context changes did not increase recognition-memory impairment beyond those observed for task-context shifts alone. Across all experiments, participants’ ability to discriminate similar lure items from studied targets (lure discrimination) was unaffected by whether the items were experienced close to event boundaries. Our findings suggest that event boundaries capable of impacting memory depend more strongly on changes that require updating of task-goals and control states than on changes in perceptual input alone. Broadly, our results indicate that not all contextual changes are functionally equivalent for event segmentation.

articles.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced-Compliance Paradigm
articles.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individual-level self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles.title: Tone Timing: An Eye-Tracking Study of Dynamic F0 Integration in Spoken Word Recognition
articles.authors: Xin Wang; Bob McMurray
articles.abstract: To recognize words, listeners must map a temporally unfolding auditory input to representations at multiple levels.  Typical accounts argue for immediate and incremental integration of asynchronous acoustic cues, such that each cue is used to partially update phonemic or lexical representations as soon as it arrives, with later cues further modulating those decisions. However, recent studies suggest that incrementality is not universal and fricatives follow a different principle in which early cues are stored in a memory buffer and listeners wait to identify the phoneme until all cues have arrived.  It is unknown why different speech sounds show these differences.  Here, we extend this paradigm to lexical tone, an acoustic/phonetic dimension which extends over a syllable and tracks the dynamics of F0.  In a visual world experiment, we index the relative activation of minimal pairs only differing in Mandarin tones as they change over time to ask whether lexical tone is incrementally integrated or processed in a buffered manner. Our findings first show lexical activation patterns are closely coupled to the timing of pitch contours, supporting the immediate integration of lexical tone.  Therefore, with respect to temporal integration of asynchronous cues, tone is like most segments, though different from fricatives.

articles.title: Formal Properties of Spontaneous Figure Drawings are Associated with Contemporaneous Affective State
articles.authors: Jake Hooper; Jennifer Mitlehner; Margaret E. Sereno
articles.abstract: Does the way a person draws reveal how they feel? Expressionist theory proposes that affect leaves traces in the formal properties of art, yet existing evidence relies largely on exceptional artists or on drawings created to depict a specified emotion. Adult participants completed a spontaneous figure drawing and reported their current affective state. Each drawing was quantified using two complementary approaches: (1) rater-coded formal elements and (2) computational image statistics. The resulting set of 40 drawing features was reduced to 9 interpretable components. Controlling for drawing time and artistic skill, these drawing components explained meaningful variance in affect, with the strongest and most robust associations emerging for negative affect. Critically, human ratings and computational image features each captured unique information not accounted for by the other, and these effects were observed in ordinary, untrained participants who were never instructed to communicate emotion. Spontaneous figure drawings thus appear to contain recoverable signatures of contemporaneous affective state embedded in their formal structure, independent of artistic skill.
