These findings position everyday drawing as an accessible, information-rich, and compact behavioral window into affect and provide a reproducible framework for quantifying how emotion is externalized in visual form.

articles.title: Usage of Digital Technology and Its linkage with the Development of Life Skills, Mental Health, and Psychological Hardiness among university students
articles.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles.abstract:
Background: The pervasive use of digital technology among Indian university students has raised concerns about its implications for life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness. While moderate use may enhance learning, excessive use is associated with adverse psychological outcomes.
Objective: This study examines (a) prevalence of digital technology usage, (b) differences in life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness across levels of digital technology usage, and (c) interlinkages among these variables.
Methods: The study adopted a two-phase design. In Phase-1, a Self-constructed Digital Technology Usage Scale was developed and standardized on 1,000 university students from Delhi-NCR. In Phase-2, data were collected from an independent sample of 600 postgraduate university students (300 professional, 300 non-professional) from government and private universities in Delhi, using stratified random sampling (Gender x Stream x University Type). Tools used: (1) Life Skills Assessment Scale (Nair et al., 2010), (2) Mental Health Inventory (Jagdish & Srivastava, 1983), and (3) Psychological Hardiness Scale (Singh, 2008).Analysis: Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, One-way ANOVA, and Multiple Regression were performed using SPSS v26.
Results: Moderate users (2-5 hrs/day) showed significantly higher life skills (M=198.60), mental health (M=158.2) and psychological hardiness (M=105.80) compared to low (<2 hrs) and high (>5 hrs) users (F=8.73 to 10.21, p<.01). Mental health (β=.38) and hardiness (β=.32) significantly predicted life skills.
Keywords: Digital Technology Usage, Life Skills, Mental Health, Psychological Hardiness, University Students

articles.title: Preliminary Evidence on Moral Underpinnings of Rape Victim Blaming in Iran: Replication and Extension of Milesi et al. (2020)
articles.authors: Mazyar Bagherian; Homa Sheibani Asl; Zohreh Hashemi Dezaki; Bahare Bahmani
articles.abstract: According to Moral Foundation Theory, people rely on five intuitive-based foundations in their moral decisions. These foundations are divided into Individualizing foundations (Care and Fairness) and Binding foundations (Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity). In an attempt to replicate Milesi at al’s (2020) findings in a non-WEIRD and honored context, across three studies, we explored the relationship between Moral Foundation and Acceptance of Modern Myths About Sexual Aggression (AMMSA) with rape victim-blaming. Study 1 showed that Fairness, Authority, and Sanctity foundations were predictive of rape victim-blaming. Study 2 showed that binding foundations predict rape victim-blaming in a preregistered analysis. Our cross-country analyses (Iran, Germany, Spain, and Italy) showed that the effects of binding moral foundations were stronger among Iranian participants than those with less-honored cultures (i.e., Italy, Spain, and Germany). Exploratory analyses revealed no differences in rape victim-blaming among men and women. However, men had higher levels of endorsement of AMMSA than women. Religious individuals had higher levels of rape victim-blaming and AMMSA. Findings are discussed concerning the honored context of Iran’s society.

articles.title: ¡Mira! How Latina Mothers use imperatives to guide children’s participation during play
articles.authors: Reinaldo Cabrera Pérez; Gustavo Carlo; Elizabeth D. Peña
articles.abstract: Maternal imperatives are often treated as a unitary form of directiveness despite serving distinct communicative functions. We examined how Spanish-speaking Latina mothers used imperatives during toy play and whether use varied by site and child gender. Forty-eight mother–child dyads from Mexico (n = 25) and the United States (n = 23) participated in semi-structured play interactions. Maternal imperatives were coded as encouragement, redirection, repetition, or scaffolding. Across 1,430 tokens, scaffolding was most frequent (36.4%), followed by encouragement (25.8%), redirection (23.6%), and repetition (14.3%). Lexical choice was strongly associated with communicative function, indicating systematic form–function patterning. Imperative use was largely similar across sites and child gender, although exploratory analyses identified greater repetition in the United States. Findings show that imperative frequency alone provides an incomplete account of maternal directiveness and underscore the importance of considering the interactional functions of direct linguistic forms.

articles.title: The relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays
articles.authors: Joonkoo Park; Shimin Hu; Ruoyu Yuan
articles.abstract: This technical note presents mathematical derivations that establish the relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays, a standard stimulus in biological and psychological research in numerosity perception (e.g., DeWind et al. (2015); Park and Huber (2022). We derive a closed-form solution for the radially averaged power spectrum of images depicting arrays of identical dots as a function of dot number, radius, spacing, and spatial frequency. We also demonstrate that an unconventional distillation of the Fourier coefficients, as done in Paul et al. (2022), reveals an artifactual relationship between that metric and numerosity.

articles.title: Representations of Change Support Object Individuation in Infancy
articles.authors: Peter Mazalik; Justin Halberda
articles.abstract:
“One can never step in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man.” This ancient puzzle by Heraclitus highlights that the world, and ourselves, are constantly changing. But to raise these puzzles, one must engage the concept of CHANGE. Developmental research shows that even infants represent highly abstract notions, including objects, agents, cause, and number. Here, we ask whether they also represent CHANGE.

We adapted the individuation paradigm pioneered by Xu and Carey (1996), in which two objects emerge sequentially from behind an occluder, preventing spatiotemporal cues about the number of objects. Infants must instead rely on contrastive featural/kind information. Prior work shows that before 12 months, infants fail to individuate objects differing in basic-level category (e.g., duck vs. truck), but succeed with broader distinctions (e.g., object vs. agent).

Here we show that infants can use the contrast between a continuously changing object and a static object to infer the number of entities present. This effect cannot be
explained by saliency alone, as infants’ longer looking at unexpected outcomes differs
from any preference for the more salient changing object, and is striking in light of
reports that infants at this age fail to individuate objects by color alone (Leslie, 1998).
Representing change opens a new avenue for research: What types of change are
encoded? Over what timescales? Embedded in which cognitive systems? By 8 months,
infants already appreciate change as a core property of the world.

articles.title: Phoneme overlap analysis of the visual benefit for speech-in-noise perception
articles.authors: John Magnotti; Yue Zhang; Lin Zhu; Yingjia Yu; Michael Beauchamp
articles.abstract:
Seeing the face of the talker improves the intelligibility of speech-in-noise, termed the visual
benefit. The visual benefit is usually measured at the whole-word level, with responses classified
as "correct" or "incorrect". An alternative method measures visual benefit using the phoneme
overlap between stimulus and response. In 55 participants presented with auditory and
audiovisual words, phoneme-overlap analysis estimated 289 different visual benefit values,
compared with only three different values for whole-word analysis. Phoneme-overlap detected a
positive visual benefit in 67% of word-participant pairs, in contrast to 32% for whole-word
analysis. Individual words varied greatly in their phoneme-overlap visual benefit, from 1% to
72%. Variability across words was accurately predicted (r = 0.78) by the phoneme composition
of the word and the visual benefit for untested words could be predicted with a median error of
9%. Measuring the visual benefit for individual phonemes revealed similarly high variability
(1% to 70%) with six phonemes (W, F, V, TH, P, AW) exhibiting visual benefit more than one
standard deviation above the mean. The increased sensitivity of phoneme-overlap analysis
relative to conventional whole-word analysis may provide a useful tool for investigating
audiovisual speech perception in clinical, neuroscience and computer science contexts.

articles.title: Robust Measurement of Habits with the Forced-Response Task A Multiverse Analysis
articles.authors: José Juan León; Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; David Luque
articles.abstract: Instrumental behavior reflects a balance between two systems: an outcome-oriented, goal-directed system and a cognitively efficient habit system that gradually gains control with repeated instrumental responding in stable contexts. While overtraining reliably induces habits in animal models, human participants often retain goal-directed control when their performance is assessed using devaluation paradigms. To address this translational gap, the forced-response method has emerged as a promising approach for studying goal-directed and habitual behavior by constraining the time available to respond. This method imposes a dual task in which participants must respond accurately to an instrumental discriminative stimulus at a specific time signaled by a sound. Because the onset of the discriminative stimulus varies across trials, the time available for response preparation is systematically manipulated. Restricting this time can unmask stimulus-driven responses when the goal-directed system has insufficient time to override them. Although the forced-response method has become increasingly popular, its use has also been accompanied by growing flexibility in data analysis, creating a potential “garden of forking paths.” Using four independent datasets, we generated 48 a priori valid preprocessing pipelines to assess variability in two discrete measures of habitual behavior—the proportion of habits and the habit index—as well as their split-half reliability and the proportion of habits as a continuous function of the available response time, modeled using generalized additive models. Results indicated that both habit measures were generally robust across preprocessing pipelines. The proportion of habits was more sensitive to specific preprocessing choices, particularly accuracy and timing-synchrony exclusion criteria, but also showed greater reliability. In all cases, however, the resulting variability was small. Reliability analyses yielded acceptable estimates in most analytic universes. Overall, these findings support the forced-response method as a robust paradigm for studying habit formation and expression in humans.

articles.title: Visuospatial Orienting in Working Memory is Preserved in Adults with ADHD Symptoms
articles.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães; Amy Louise Atkinson; Richard John Allen; Valerie Camos
articles.abstract: People with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are reported to have pervasive deficits in working memory (WM), yet mechanistic explanations for such deficits are lacking. Research suggests that attentional mechanisms such as reward-based prioritisation and visuospatial orienting are intact in this population (Atkinson et al., 2025; Superbia-Guimarães et al., 2022, 2023). To further examine these mechanisms, we investigated the hypotheses that deficient visuospatial orienting during encoding and maintenance are at the root of WM deficits in adults with ADHD symptoms.  Eighty-four symptomatic participants (Mage = 28.4 years, SD = 4.6) and 107 controls (Mage = 29.4, SD = 4.4) had their symptoms assessed with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. They each took part in one of two experiments involving an item (colour or unfamiliar shape) recognition memory task that incorporated pre- and retro-cues. Across both experiments, we found strong evidence of beneficial pre- and retro-cueing effects upon memory accuracy and reaction time (RT). However, we found no evidence for the expected group differences nor the interaction between symptom status and cueing condition. There was also no evidence for correlations between ADHD symptom scores, recognition accuracy, RT, and cueing benefits. Therefore, attentional mechanisms are unlikely to explain deficits in WM in individuals with symptoms of ADHD.

articles.title: The ontogenesis of socio-affective touch perception: Assessing valence and inferring social relationships from observed tactile interactions.
articles.authors: Louise P Kirsch; Monica Nkele; Adeline Depierreux; Olivier Mascaro
articles.abstract:
Social touch is a powerful communication channel conveying social dispositions and affiliative relationships across the primate lineage. Yet, how social inferences from observed socio-affective touch develop remains poorly understood. Three complementary experiments with 217 children aged 3 to 6 and 144 adults address this gap.
Experiment 1 tested the ability to assess the valence of observed tactile interactions. By age 3, children accurately evaluated a range of positive and negative touch interactions, integrating multiple cues, including the recipient of the touch (object vs. person) and stroke speed—consistent with key properties of skin afferents that process touch. Valence evaluation of observed touch thus emerges early.
Experiments 2a-2b examined children's and adults' ability to infer social bonds from observed touch. Participants watched two actresses: one stroked a character, while the other performed a matched neutral gesture (no touch, or touch at very fast speed). From around age 4, children consistently judged the stroking actress as more likely to be affiliated with the touched character—but only with that specific character, not with a different one. Adults, by contrast, generalized this inference, expecting affiliation between the stroking actress and characters beyond the one she had touched.
These findings reveal a developmental progression in processing observed social touch, from valence detection, to relationship-specific inference, to generalized trait attribution. Thus, observed-touch processing relies not on one unified ability but on a multilevel system with distinct developmental timelines—underscoring touch's central role in social cognition and the need for further research bridging these domains.

articles.title: Maladaptive Personality Traits and Statement Validity Assessment. Mapping DSM-5 Trait Domains and Facets onto Lying, Suggestibility, and Autobiographical Memory Quality
articles.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Merle Hurtmanns; Johannes Zimmermann
articles.abstract: Statement validity assessment (SVA) requires experts to weigh a witness’s personality when judging motives for deception, expectable statement quality, and suggestibility. We propose the maladaptive trait model of the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders as a common language for these steps and test its expectations with low-stakes paradigms at the domain and facet level. In a German community sample (N = 258), we administered the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Short Form, a matrix cheating task, the Lying in Everyday Situations scale, an online Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scale, and self-ratings of memory quality and imagery vividness. We report correlations between all 5 domains and 25 facets with all criteria, with confidence intervals, false-discovery-rate correction, and Bayes factors. Self-reported lying was positively related to Antagonism and Disinhibition, with motive-specific patterns; contrary to preregistration, so was Negative Affectivity. Memory clarity and imagery vividness were related to Detachment, Negative Affectivity, and several of their facets. No trait was related to behavioral dishonesty or suggestibility; Bayes factors mostly favored the null. Facets improved cross-validated prediction where they diverged from their domain. For SVA, the results support using antagonistic and self-protective profiles in motive analysis and lowering expectations of detail and vividness for detached and depressive witnesses.

articles.title: Perceived punitive consequences and adolescent violent crime: The moderating role of socio-legal legitimacy in a Brazilian birth cohort
articles.authors: Andreas Bauer; Justice Tankebe; Thaís Martins-Silva; Alicia Matijasevich; Aluísio J. D. Barros; Iná Santos; Luciana Tovo Rodrigues; Joseph Murray
articles.abstract: Research on legitimacy and crime is dominated by cross-sectional evidence from high-income countries. Furthermore, less is known about how legitimacy and deterrence jointly shape adolescent violence in fragile institutional contexts. Using longitudinal data from the 2004 Pelotas Birth Cohort Study in Brazil (n = 1,510), a population-based, prospective longitudinal study, we examine whether perceived punitive consequences and three legitimacy dimensions — regarding the police, the law, and the social system — are associated with violent crime at ages 15 and 18. Higher perceived punitive consequences and more positive perceptions of legitimacy across all domains were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 15, whereas only police legitimacy and perceived punitive consequences were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 18. Legitimacy of the law and of the social system moderated the association between perceived punitive consequences and violent crime at age 15, with negative associations strongest among adolescents who viewed institutions as less legitimate. These findings suggest that legitimacy is multidimensional and that both normative and instrumental processes jointly shape adolescent violence in high-violence contexts.

articles.title: Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis: The PIMMA Framework
articles.authors: Matteo Manente; Livio Finos; Gianmarco Altoè; Filippo Gambarota
articles.abstract: Meta-analyses, like primary studies, are affected by researcher degrees of freedom: researchers must decide which studies to include, how to compute effect sizes, and which statistical models to use. Different reasonable choices can lead to different results, making multiverse meta-analysis a useful tool for assessing robustness across alternative specifications. However, multiverse meta-analysis also introduces a multiple-testing problem. Current inferential approaches mainly provide a global test, which can establish that at least one specification differs from the null but cannot identify which individual specifications do so while accounting for multiplicity across the full multiverse. We introduce Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis (PIMMA), which allows inference on individual specifications while controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) and accounting for their dependence. In practical terms, PIMMA shows which results remain statistically significant after accounting for multiplicity across all reasonable analytical choices. In simulations, the specification-level test adequately controlled Type I error, with power comparable to robust variance estimation in scenarios where both methods maintained appropriate Type I error control. In an application to meta-analyses of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy efficacy for adult depression, 297 of 336 unique meta-analytic analyses remained significant after step-down max-T adjustment for multiple testing, accounting for dependence among analyses. PIMMA therefore extends multiverse meta-analysis from a global assessment of whether any effect is present to specification-level inference, allowing researchers to evaluate robustness across specifications and identify which individual results remain significant under appropriate error control.

articles.title: Gesturing at the Boundary: Can Concurrent Beat Gestures Bias Speech Segmentation?
articles.authors: Huandi Chen; Hans Rutger Bosker
articles.abstract: Beat gestures, rhythmic hand movements that reliably co-occur with prosodically prominent syllables, are one of the most common types of gestures in everyday conversations. Given their coupling to speech prosody, they can influence stress perception and facilitate lexical access. Still, little is known about their contribution to speech segmentation. Recent work has shown that beat gestures conveying distinct rhythms in a precursor (i.e., distal context) can bias the segmentation of subsequently presented acoustically ambiguous speech (Bosker, 2026). However, whether a single beat gesture co-occurring with the ambiguous speech (i.e., proximal context) can similarly shift boundary placement remains unknown. Across two experiments, participants segmented acoustically ambiguous four-syllable sequences (e.g., cry sister nip vs. crisis turnip) while a beat gesture was aligned to either the second or third syllable. Unexpectedly, no reliable effect of gesture placement on segmentation was observed. These findings suggest that isolated beat gestures may not function as reliable independent cues to speech segmentation. Instead, their influence may depend on the broader audiovisual and rhythmic context.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Sharing:   Reconsidering the Role of Traditional Femininity/masculinity
articles.authors: X. Jia; Annet Kleiboer; Karen Holtmaat; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: A substantial body of research indicates that men, on average, share emotions less readily than women. The current research examined the extent to which gender differences in traditional femininity and traditional masculinity account for this relationship. In Study 1, 1,500 Dutch adults (938 women and 562 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (Distress Disclosure Index, DDI; Kahn & Hessling, 2001), gender self-concept (Dutch Gender self-concept Questionnaire, NSIV; Willemsen & Fischer, 1996), and self-stigma towards help-seeking (Self-Stigma of Seeking Help Scale, SSOSH; Vogel et al., 2006). In Study 2, 1,645 Dutch adults (979 women and 666 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (DDI), gender self-concept (Bem Sex Role Inventory, BSRI; Bem, 1981), and help-seeking intentions (General Help Seeking Questionnaire, GHSQ; Wilson et al., 2005). Gender differences in emotional sharing were consistently partially explained by traditional femininity, but not by traditional masculinity. The same pattern emerged for help-seeking self-stigma (Study 1) and intentions (Study 2). These findings contradict widespread beliefs that traditional masculinity keeps men from disclosing their emotional vulnerabilities and seeking mental healthcare. More generally, the present findings highlight gender self-concept as a valuable theoretical concept in understanding the psychology of emotional sharing.

articles.title: Exploring the Role of Transportation and Narrative Persuasion in Historical Virtual Reality from a Democratic Education Perspective
articles.authors: Lea Frentzel-Beyme; Hannah Decker; Nicole Krämer
articles.abstract: Virtual  reality  (VR)  is  increasingly  used  in  history  education  to  enable  immersive  engagement  with  the  past.  Although  these  applications  may  stimulate  interest  and  emotional  involvement, concerns have been raised about their potential to hinder critical reflection and foster  uncritical  acceptance  of  story-consistent  beliefs.  Drawing  on  the  transportation-imagery  model,  the  present  study  (N  =  106)  investigates  the  correlations  between  transportation  (i.e.,  narrative  immersion)  in  the  history-related  VR  application  Anne  Frank  House  VR  and  users’  emotional  responses,  knowledge,  and  story-consistent  political  beliefs.  Special  attention  is  paid  to  the  role  of  users’  political  orientation.  The  results  indicate  that  transportation is positively correlated with emotional responses and story-consistent beliefs (e.g., support for refugees) but not with factual or perceived knowledge. These findings point to the persuasive potential and educational opportunities offered by VR for history education. Although VR may not convey knowledge, it may foster engagement with socially and politically relevant topics.

articles.title: Attention Fragmentation: Toward a Formal Construct Definition, a Differentiated Nomological Network, and a Research Agenda for Scale Development
articles.authors: Diksha Sharma; Pooja Tyagi
articles.abstract: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar & Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

articles.title: Discussing Racial Demographic Change Online: Constructive Discourse Is Prevalent, Rewarded, and Propagated
articles.authors: Jonathan Doriscar; Anika Wilsnack; Tessa Charlesworth
articles.abstract: Racial demographic change is transforming the United States away from a White majority, a shift that can make concerns about group status especially salient. Public responses increasingly unfold in online video comment spaces, which are often perceived as ubiquitously hostile and toxic. Using 14 years of YouTube and TikTok comments (N = 101,103) responding to 106 high-engagement videos, we operationalize two discourse-feature indices: destructive features (e.g., toxicity and identity attacks) and constructive features (e.g., compassion and curiosity). We find that constructive features were: (1) 2.6x more prevalent than destructive features; (2) associated with YouTube engagement, where each unit increase corresponded to 3x more likes and 5x more replies; and (3) propagated in reply chains, with constructive parent comments followed by more constructive replies. Constructiveness is distinct from mere positive sentiment, politeness, agreement, or stance on diversity, and is a widely-prevalent discourse style for climate change. Hostile online content is not what is produced, rewarded, or propagated in the majority of content.

articles.title: Local average treatment effects on latent outcomes
articles.authors: Sanford R Student; Joshua B Gilbert; William Young
articles.abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) regression models for causal inference have received increased attention in psychology with continuous, observed variables. Yet, latent outcomes are ubiquitous in psychology and research designs involving non-binding treatments and encouragement/manipulation designs are widespread. We consider IV with a binary instrument and treatment to estimate the \textit{local average treatment effect} on a latent variable, or the latent local average treatment effect (LLATE). The LLATE is the average of heterogeneous latent treatment effects for the population of individuals who comply with treatment assignment. Heterogeneous treatment effects imply that a single-group SEM with residual normality of the outcome is misspecified. We propose a multiple-group estimator that allows for this heteroskedasticity, enables tests for heterogeneous treatment effects, and characterizes compliers. The multiple-group estimator recovers the LLATE with trivial bias, while two single-group estimators and a two-step procedure using factor score estimates as observed outcomes all yield small but persistent bias. Testing for heterogeneous treatment effects is possible but limited to larger samples. We conclude that IV with a latent outcome is a viable means of estimating causal effects on latent outcomes, and that the multiple-group approach is usually the safest way to do so.

articles.title: When the self is on display: How narcissism shapes facial and emotional responses to social feedback during personal storytelling
articles.authors: Matias Piispanen; Jarno Tuominen; Ville Johannes Harjunen; Emmi Koskinen; Mariel Wuolio; Elizabeth Krusemark; Pärttyli Rinne; Mikko Sams; Anssi Peräkylä; Juha Salmitaival
articles.abstract: Personal storytelling exposes identity-relevant aspects of the self to social evaluation. Narcissism provides a characteristic example of elevated sensitivity to interpersonal evaluation and need for social validation. We examined responses to face-affirming and face-threatening feedback on personal narratives in grandiose and vulnerable narcissism to clarify individual differences in managing such exposure. In line with our hypothesis, data from 177 participants showed that higher narcissistic traits predict heightened nonverbal responses and altered self-reported emotional responses. Machine-learning analysis of video data revealed increased activation of the lip corner puller (AU12) in individuals higher in grandiose narcissism, reflecting enhanced outward signalling through greater smiling in response to both positive and negative feedback. Self-reports indicated heightened pride in grandiose narcissism, whereas vulnerable narcissism was associated with more negative subjective experiences, including lower pride, valence, and dominance, which were not reflected in facial expressions. Our findings shed light on how narcissistic traits may shape the use of facial expressions as strategic tools for impression management under social evaluation.

articles.title: Scene and Heard: Spatial layout and verbal labels support young infants’ categorization of places
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Agata Bochynska; Daniel D. Dilks; Moira Rose Dillon; LDM@NYU
articles.abstract: Human infants are limited in their self-guided navigation. Can they nevertheless learn about the places they’ll go? Three experiments examined pre-crawling 6-month-old infants’ (N = 96; 45 girls and 51 boys) ability to categorize places using a novelty-preference looking-time paradigm. During familiarization, infants saw videos presenting forward and backward motion through places from the same category: either fields, which have an open spatial layout; or canyons, which have a closed spatial layout. At test, they saw two videos side by side in silence: a new place from the familiar category and a place from a novel category. When each place was labeled with the same novel noun during familiarization in Experiment 1, infants looked longer at the novel place category at test, suggesting their sensitivity to places’ distinct spatial layouts and an ability to learn place categories. When the places’ spatial layouts were scrambled in Experiment 2, infants attended more to the places’ low-level features, disrupting their place categorization. When the places were presented in silence in Experiment 3, infants showed no evidence of place categorization. These results reveal infants’ sensitivity to category-relevant place information, especially with verbal labels, and their ability to learn place categories prior to self-guided exploration.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: Embedding qualitative data in LLM semantic space: A tutorial on conceptualization, measurement, and validation
articles.authors: Toshizumi Muta
articles.abstract: Large language model embeddings give any text coordinates in a semantic space, where the cosine between two coordinates indexes their similarity. Standard qualitative practice cannot quantify such closeness: open-ended answers become nominal variables, which represent only difference under dummy codes. Psychometrics obtains such closeness from responses, as the correlations among a scale's items. Whether the cosine can substitute for the correlation is therefore open. We tested it against established findings in open data, each with an agreed structure: the Big Five, PANAS in two languages, Schwartz's values, Pineo-Porter occupational prestige, and the ISEAR and Kjell narratives. Linguistic structure alone did not reproduce the psychometric structure. The item texts recovered part of it, and none of it where a relation carries a sign. They fall far short of a random split-sample ceiling. Read from the other side, that is a finding about questionnaires: a scale's wording does not carry what its respondents give it. Embeddings supply a semantic layer between raw language and conventional coding, where the material that neither psychometrics nor hand coding reaches belongs. A category label—an occupation, a diagnosis, a brand—becomes coordinates rather than a dummy variable. An open-ended answer becomes coordinates without a coder. Cut into segments, a long answer becomes a path, along which departures, returns, and drifts can be drawn and tested. What any of it means, however, stays with the analyst. We supply the conceptual background, an R package, and a tutorial: no training, no Python.

articles.title: Public attention to artificial intelligence predicts helping between humans across 86 countries
articles.authors: Chenxi Li; Xiaoxue Hu; Xue Wang; Mengchen Dong
articles.abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has provoked debate about its consequences for human social life. Yet, whether and how public attention to AI shapes human relationships globally are largely unknown. In a global online game, we linked daily country-level AI attention from Google Trends to more than 1.5 million player-day records of voluntary helping among 9,167 players across 86 countries. Higher national attention to AI predicted increased helping behavior between players, an association robust across samples, measures, and specifications. This link was corroborated by quasi-experimental analyses around OpenAI DevDay, a major AI event, showing that helping rose in proportion to countries’ attention responses and shifted upward at the event date. The response was stronger where a shared human identity was likely salient and AI-related change likely felt pressing. Amid narratives casting AI as a threat to humanity, strengthened interpersonal bonds may mark a collective human adaptation to its rise.

articles.title: The prose penalty in AI-assisted authorship
articles.authors: Faisal Feroz; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Jim Albert Charlton Everett; Sebastian Porsdam Mann; Brian D. Earp
articles.abstract: Generative AI based on large language models (LLMs) is increasingly used in academic, journalistic, and other professional and online writing, yet its implications for human authorship remain contested. We asked whether assignment of authorship credit depends on which task within the larger writing process a writer delegates to an AI assistant; whether any observed credit penalty is unique to AI; and whether credit can be restored through personalization: using an AI trained on one’s own previous writing. Across two preregistered studies (N = 878 US participants), observers evaluated a writer who either wrote unaided or delegated brainstorming, outlining, drafting, editing/revising, fact-checking, or all five tasks to an LLM or human assistant. In Study 1, although delegating a single task reduced authorship credit on average, the largest penalty by far applied to delegated drafting of prose, regardless of whether the helper was human or AI. Only the perceived originality needed for each task was independently associated with differences in credit assignment; perceived effort and skill were not. Perceived writing quality was also lower with LLM than human assistance, despite evaluated passages being randomly drawn from the same pool. In Study 2, using an LLM personalized on the writer’s own prior work increased both authorship credit and perceived writing quality relative to using a standard LLM. These findings show that authorship judgments depended principally on whether the writer produced the prose, regardless of helper type; that credit tracks judgments of originality, rather than effort or skill; and that the “prose penalty” on authorship attributions in AI-assisted writing can be partially reduced through personalization.

articles.title: Facing Trust: How Anthropomorphism and Individual Differences Shape Perceptions of Robot Faces
articles.authors: Lian Fingal; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Trust is essential to the development and maintenance of human relationships, and perceptions of trust based on the face alone can occur in as little as 100ms. Humans also tend to make trust estimations of robots based on their physical design, and these assessments can lead to successful acceptance of the robot or result in rejection. As robots are being designed to integrate into our daily lives, examining the factors that contribute to robot trustworthiness is a crucial component to understanding Human-Robot Interactions (HRI). Anthropomorphism is the attribution of human-likeness to objects, and it is suggested that imbuing robots with human characteristics can facilitate perceptions of trustworthiness. This study investigated the association of anthropomorphism with perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces and whether there is a potentially predictive role of the tendency to anthropomorphise that would mediate trustworthiness perceptions. 43 participants rated their impressions of 30 robot images on trustworthiness and human-likeness. Participants also completed the individual differences in anthropomorphism questionnaire (IDAQ; Waytz et al., 2010). We hypothesised that anthropomorphic ratings on the Godspeed Anthropomorphism questionnaire (Bartneck, Kulić, et al., 2009) would be associated with perceptions of trustworthiness on a single item measure of trustworthiness. We did not find support for this hypothesis (r(41) = .041, p = .795, N = 43). We hypothesised that individual differences in the tendency to anthropomorphise would be associated with human-likeness of robot faces. We found that IDAQ scores were not associated with anthropomorphism (Estimate = .219, S.E. = .286, C.R. = .766, p = .444). Finally, we hypothesised that individual differences would mediate the relationship between anthropomorphism and  perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces. We found that there was no significant relationship between IDAQ scores and trustworthiness perceptions (Estimate = -.005, S.E. = .135, C.R. = -.039, p = .969). These findings suggest that participants accessed prior negative knowledge about robots and applied them to the robot images in this study. Additionally, the results suggest that trust affordances cannot be detected simply in the physical features of a robot. Limitations include the experimental design, especially the one-item measure of trustworthiness and the lack of contextual cues.

articles.title: Intergenerational differences and inheritance of marriage between born “around 1975” and “after-1995” groups based on China
articles.authors: Jingxi Zheng; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Marriage is a union under socialised norms, the typical model being monogamy. It provides for the smooth development of society and a perennially active economic market. The globalised rise in late marriage and divorce rates is to some extent a reflection of life choices and attitudes towards marriage. China is a densely populated country, and after the one-child policy, most families has a pyramidal structure; in 2021, the Chinese government officially enacted the three-child policy, with the aim of stimulating and encouraging people to have more children. However, with the rapid development of the economy, modernisation and industrialisation, there are dynamic changes of individuals’ consideration. The target group for this study is parents who have experienced a change in fertility policy who born around 1975, and their children, the millennials born after 1995. Seven pairs of families were recruited to join the study through snowball sampling. The study used a qualitative approach, with volunteers first completing a demographic questionnaire; semi-structured interviews allowed participants to explore and consider in depth, and asynchronous interviews compensated for the fact that some participants were unable to have simultaneous one-to-one communication online. The researcher forms four themes: the importance of marriage, love and cruelty in marriage, opposite sex kinship and mate choice, and women in marriage. The analysis concluded that there are indeed similarities and contradictions in intergenerational perceptions of marriage, as well as differences between individuals and family units. Inheritance is mainly in the identification of marital behaviour and marital and family pressures, and differences revolve around the two generations' starting points for marriage and attitudes to non-mainstream marriage trends. However, parental influence on children is also externalised into acting styles such as reinforcement, correction, and avoidance to spousal choices due to the unique patterns of the individual internalised system.

articles.title: Pop-Culture Psychopathy: How Media Exposure Affects Laypersons’ Recognition of Clinical Psychopathic Traits
articles.authors: Robyn Marshall; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Entertainment media has proven to be an essential source of information about mental disorders and crucial in educating the public about these conditions. Consequently, how the media portrays the mentally ill is very important, yet they continue to be depicted alongside images of violence and crime. Psychopathy has been portrayed as a disorder of deceit, manipulation and charm despite research continually confirming otherwise. The inaccurate portrayals of psychopathy have far-reaching consequences, most alarmingly in the criminal justice system. These ‘psychopaths’ work alongside stigmatisation, categorisation theories and social learning and cultivation theories to encourage false beliefs about the disorder. This study uses a quantitative approach, collecting responses to a questionnaire through social media, to investigate the influence of inaccurate media depictions on the layperson’s ability to diagnose psychopathy accurately. The study compares psychopathy to participants’ ability to diagnose antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia. The author then looks for a relationship between participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy, their confidence in their knowledge about psychopathy and their interaction with media depictions of psychopaths before finally investigating the influence of several demographic characteristics. A non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA revealed that participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy is significantly worse than their ability to recognise the other conditions in vignettes. A multiple linear regression analysis revealed that a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy increased as their confidence increased and decreased as their media diversity score increased, however only the relationship between ability to identify and confidence was significant. Finally, multiple ANOVAs revealed that age and previous psychological knowledge had a significant impact on a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy accurately.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Bringing our tribes together:  The promise and peril of interdisciplinary research on epistemically suspect beliefs
articles.authors: Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Raunak M Pillai; Steve Rathje
articles.abstract: Epistemically suspect beliefs are studied across multiple disciplines, yet these literatures have developed largely in parallel. We argue that integrating research from clinical, social, cognitive, and political psychology offers an important opportunity to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the origins and consequences of these beliefs. In particular, research on social identity can help explain how people select information and social environments, evaluate evidence, and process information in ways that affirm their identities. Extending these insights to clinical contexts raises new questions about how social and personal identities shape susceptibility to certain beliefs, including in emerging information environments shaped by artificial intelligence. However, interdisciplinary research faces substantial institutional and psychological barriers. Academic incentives often reward disciplinary competition, simple theories, and surprising findings over integration, encouraging researchers to defend disciplinary identities and caricature competing perspectives. Building a robust science of beliefs therefore requires a culture of cooperation that prioritizes explanatory utility and theoretical synthesis over disciplinary dominance, and needs to be supported by interdisciplinary funding, hiring, training, conferences, and journals.

articles.title: The Form Composition Hypothesis: When Concepts Combine, Their Central Forms Are Privileged
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Human cognition involves the rapid combining of concepts to generate complex meaning, as in natural language. However, conceptual combination leads to a Massive Ambiguity Problem: since vast amounts of information are stored within each concept, even simple combinations can have many potential meanings. This paper introduces the Form Composition Hypothesis, a proposal within Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure. On Form Theory, every concept has a central form, a structure with a special cross-domain format for storing a compressed subset of each concept’s conceptual information, which then gives that information default influence within human cognition. The Form Composition Hypothesis proposes that when concepts are combined, the human mind uses this cross-domain format to limit the initial set of possible meanings. Across four sets of experiments, participants consistently prioritized form interpretations over non-form interpretations for familiar sentences, novel sentences, and sentences involving both familiar and novel concepts. Importantly, they judged non-form interpretations to be impossible in context-free tasks, providing evidence that non-form interpretations may require additional processing, and they spontaneously generated form interpretations in open-ended tasks. It is argued that form composition acts as a generative, structural constraint on conceptual combination, providing the structural conditions for linguistic creativity. The framework also has implications for communication and reasoning errors, concept learning, generative language models, and the human tendency toward reductive reasoning.

articles.title: Dynamics of Perceived Rejection in Everyday Life
articles.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Haya Fatimah; Marina Bornovalova; Lijuan Wang; Fallon Rachael Goodman
articles.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal rejection is typically studied using trait questionnaires or in laboratory settings, while its temporal dynamics that may characterize important individual differences are often overlooked. This study examined perceived rejection in daily life as a dynamic process and its specificity from negative affect.

Method: 89 community adults, including 46 with DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), completed a 28-day EMA protocol with five prompts per day, yielding 9279 observations after data screening. Dynamic structural equation modeling was used to estimate equilibrium (typical level), inertia (persistence over time), innovation variance (magnitude of momentary perturbations), and stationary variance (overall within-person variability) for perceived rejection.

Results: Perceived rejection dynamics were associated with negative affect dynamics. After controlling for the corresponding negative affect components, SAD diagnosis and several interpersonal vulnerability measures (e.g., separation anxiety) remained associated with perceived rejection dynamics. When SAD diagnosis and interpersonal vulnerabilities were considered together, separation anxiety was uniquely associated with higher equilibrium, greater inertia, and greater stationary variance, whereas SAD was uniquely associated with greater log innovation variance; need to belong and rejection sensitivity were additionally associated with higher equilibrium.

Conclusions: Perceived rejection appears to reflect a distinct interpersonal dynamic process beyond negative affect. Within this process, a person’s typical level of perceived rejection, momentary perturbations, the persistence of deviations from the person’s typical level, and overall variability showed different patterns of association with SAD and interpersonal vulnerabilities, suggesting that these dynamic features capture different aspects of perceived rejection.

articles.title: Reducing Measurement Error in Forecaster Evaluation Using the Wisdom of Crowds
articles.authors: Jessica Helmer; Nikolay Petrov; Sophie Ma Zhu; Ezra Karger; Edgar C. Merkle; Mark Himmelstein
articles.abstract:
Forecasting skill is often measured by the average error between forecasters’ predictions and the ground truth, but the inherent uncertainty in event outcomes adds an additional layer of measurement error onto skill estimation. Intersubjective measures offer an alternative approach to skill measurement: comparing forecasters’ predictions to those of their peers, typically to aggregated forecasts from groups of peers. A key advantage of this approach is that forecasts can be scored in real time, without having to wait for the ground truth outcome to be realized. However, it has another more subtle advantage as well: aggregate predictions can be less noisy than ground truth outcomes, leading to a potential reduction in this additional
measurement error. In a simulation study, we demonstrate conditions under which crowd aggregates provide a more reliable indicator of the optimal forecast for a given event than a single realized ground truth outcome, leading to skill measurement with reduced measurement error. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of intersubjective methods in a real-world forecasting study in which 894 participants made both forecasts and metapredictions, i.e., predictions of what others might forecast. As in our simulation, intersubjective measures capture forecasting ability more efficiently than do ground-truth scores, demonstrating their usefulness for identifying high-performing forecasters.

articles.title: Fear, Conformity, and Phantom Majorities
articles.authors: Cory J Clark
articles.abstract:
In many ways, modern human brains are not adapted to modern environments, and our social worlds are one of the most significant evolutionary mismatches. Humans evolved in small-scale interdependent tribes, where information about local peer networks was observable or obtainable through mutual acquaintances. In such environments, people would have relatively good information about the prevalence of certain beliefs (a numerator) and a clear sense of their network size (a denominator), and thus could assess the relative popularity of different views and values. This assessment of majority views would help humans navigate their social worlds, allowing them to conform to popular beliefs and values or at least avoid visible violations of those beliefs and values. Given the small size of these environments, if dozens or hundreds of people appeared to support a particular perspective–and especially if one did not share that perspective–that perspective would be socially important and warrant consideration.
In modern environments, and particularly on social media, we routinely encounter views endorsed (via likes and reshares) by dozens, hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of people, where those seemingly popular views might represent <1% of the people who saw and thus could have endorsed the content. Human psychology is not adapted to intuit that thousands of people might be a socially insignificant percentage of people. I refer to these illusory crowds as “phantom majorities”: psychologically imposing masses of people that are experienced as far more representative of a population (and thus far more socially powerful) than they are in reality. In this short essay, I contend that (1) outgroup phantom majorities have contributed to exaggerated negative perceptions of outgroups and reactive extremism, and (2) ingroup phantom majorities have contributed to self-censorship, preference falsification, and mistargeted viewpoint conformity. Because both ingroup and outgroup phantom majorities can polarize, they may also contribute to self-fulfilling prophecies whereby seemingly popular fringe views become more popular, increasing their prevalence on social media and feeding back through the cycle.

articles.title: A World-Model Theory of Trait Anxiety
articles.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Joel G. Thomas; Noa Yadid; Dafna Yavetz
articles.abstract: Computational psychiatry has sought the mechanisms of anxiety in domain-general biases in learning and planning, and found small, inconsistent effects. We argue this is because trait anxiety is not a bias in how a person learns any task but a property of the person's world model, namely the beliefs they hold about threat, control, and the self in particular domains, and the strategies that bring those beliefs to bear on a situation. We formalize a world model as comprising causal knowledge, an intrinsic reward function, available actions, and internal strategies, and build a minimal generative model in which each has a concrete role in explaining common trait anxiety behaviors. Most importantly, the model inverts the usual place of generalization. Instead of asking whether a task's findings generalize to real-world conditions, it models how far a person's real-world beliefs generalize to the task, and treats the computational parameters of learning and planning that a task measures as contingent on that generalization. Simulations demonstrate how, within tasks similar-enough to the domains of core anxious beliefs, avoidance behavior and anxious thought can arise in qualitatively distinct ways by virtue of world model components. We review prior attempts to relate trait anxiety to computations of learning and planning using our model, and argue that, to advance the field, future studies should personalize cognitive tasks based on threat-related world model content.

articles_hidden.title: Unjust World Theory: A Tripartite Model of Justice Worldviews and the Moralization of Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Gabrielle Ibasco; Azim Shariff
articles_hidden.abstract: The just world belief (JWB)—the heuristic that people get what they deserve—has long explained why people may legitimize social inequality. However, far less has been theorized about the other side of the coin: believing in an unjust world. Rather than the unjust world belief merely reflecting the absence of the JWB, we explicate a typology of three distinct justice worldviews, or psychological lenses for interpreting and responding to an unequal status quo. In addition to the JWB, we introduce the non-just world belief (non-JWB; outcomes are randomly determined, uncorrelated with deservingness) and the anti-just world belief (anti-JWB; people get what they least deserve). Across 8 studies leveraging 12 unique samples (N = 20,777), we used correlational, longitudinal and experimental designs to evidence the functions and consequences of each worldview. In Studies 1-3 (Construct), we establish that the two unjust world beliefs are distinct from each other and from the JWB, and are relatively stable dispositions that meaningfully track differences in status. In Studies 4–5 (Profile), we show that the non-JWB captures a morally unstructured worldview associated with epistemic uncertainty and diminished meaning in life, whereas the anti-JWB captures an existentially coherent yet critical orientation toward power. Consequently, in Studies 6–8 (Implications), the anti-JWB, over and above the JWB, predicts opposition to social inequality in both attitudes and voting behaviors, particularly when such opposition involves disempowering the socioeconomic elite. Together, these findings contribute to an understanding of distinct routes through which people appraise and respond to inequality.

articles_hidden.title: Faculty Evaluations of DEI Statements for Academic Hiring
articles_hidden.authors: Nathan Honeycutt
articles_hidden.abstract: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (“DEI”) statements have become a popular additional evaluative criterion for academic hiring and promotion, but little to no empirical research has been conducted to assess how university faculty evaluate these statements. The present set of experiments sought to fill this void. Across seven studies (ntotal=4,953), tenured/tenure-track university faculty rated DEI statements that did not discuss race/ethnicity and gender diversity actions or efforts (i.e., statements that lacked equalitarian content) significantly lower than those that did. Specifically, faculty perceived these “alternative” statements to be weaker DEI statements, and perceived the applicants who submitted these statements to be less competent, less hireable, and less likable. Furthermore, faculty were less likely to recommend–often by a large margin–that the applicants behind these “alternative” statements pass an initial screening and be advanced for further review. Evaluative penalties were most severe toward DEI statements focusing only on viewpoint diversity actions and efforts (Studies 1-4), but also manifested for statements focusing only on rural diversity (Study 6), or only on socioeconomic diversity (Study 7). Findings for disability diversity (Study 5) were mixed. These studies provide novel insight on how DEI statements are perceived and evaluated by university faculty.

articles_hidden.title: The precision hierarchy hypothesis: A unifying framework to explain opposing serial effects
articles_hidden.authors: Carina Ufer; Helen Blank
articles_hidden.abstract: Serial dependence, the phenomenon where current perception is biased toward the previous stimulus, has been interpreted as a mechanism for perceptual stability, smoothing variability in sensory input. However, analyses that include both the previous stimulus and previous response unmasked repulsive effects at the sensory level that were otherwise concealed. Moreover, attractive serial biases fail to scale with environmental correlations, challenging their primary role in maintaining stability. We propose the Precision hierarchy hypothesis, grounded in predictive processing, as a unifying framework for these seemingly contradictory findings. Repulsive effects naturally emerge when priors - shaped by recent trials - are highly precise, making small deviations in incoming input more probable under alternative priors. We further propose that prior precision decreases across hierarchical levels. A higher precision at lower sensory levels leads to repulsive effects, as even small deviations in incoming signal are in conflict with the prior. In contrast, attractive biases emerge at higher, more abstract levels, where deviations are integrated with broader conceptual priors. By dynamically shaping prior precision according to environmental correlations, perception remains adaptive, balancing the need for stability with the sensitivity to detect meaningful changes in the environment. This framework reconciles diverse findings on serial effects and provides testable predictions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: The Neurophysiology of Binding and Retrieval in Action Control and Its Alterations in Tourette Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Beste; Christian Frings; Alexander Munchau
articles_hidden.abstract: Goal-directed behavior requires that perception and action are bound together and coordinated so that what we perceive can be translated into appropriate actions. The Binding and Retrieval in Action Control (BRAC) framework describes this process as a dynamic interplay between two complementary operations: binding and retrieval. Understanding the neurophysiology of these processes has become a central aspect of cognitive neuroscience. Recent evidence links them to the rhythmic synchronization of neural activity - oscillations in the theta, alpha, and beta frequency ranges - that coordinate distributed cortical and subcortical networks. These oscillations provide a temporal code that allows the brain to integrate information across space and time while flexibly reconfiguring internal representations. The second part of this chapter applies the BRAC framework to Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome (GTS). Traditionally viewed as a motor-inhibition disorder, GTS is increasingly recognized as a condition of altered perception-action integration. Empirical findings reveal that event-file bindings in GTS are excessively strong or unstable and that the oscillatory coordination underlying their regulation is disturbed. By tracing the links between rhythmic neural dynamics and behavioral control, BRAC offers a mechanistic bridge between basic neurophysiology and the clinical phenomenology of tics.

articles_hidden.title: Recommendations & Caveats for Recruiting Stratified Samples Across Race/Ethnicity, Gender, and Socioeconomic Status Using the Prolific Online Platform
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Machina; Kimberly A. Muellers; Xiqiao Chen; E. Samuel Winer
articles_hidden.abstract: Though online sampling methods have progressed, psychology literature continues to include primarily white, educated, upper-class samples. This work will outline the methodology of a stratified community study examining demographic differences in fear of happiness and depression among U.S. adults. Drawing on prior research suggesting variation in emotional processes across social identities, we implemented a fully crossed stratified sampling design to ensure equal representation across race/ethnicity (Black, Asian, Latine, White), gender (cisgender male, cisgender female), and socioeconomic status (SES). Eligible participants were 18-65 years old and residing in the U.S. SES categories were defined as ≤ $50,000 (low), $50,000 - $100,000 (middle), and ≥ $100,000 (high). A priori power analysis (G*Power) indicated a target of 42 participants per cell (N=1,008) to detect medium effects. Following the exclusion of 75 uncategorizable cases, the per-cell target was adjusted to 38, maintaining adequate power for medium-to-large effects. Participants were recruited in SES-based blocks via Prolific. Procedures to preserve stratification, confidentiality, and analytic rigor will be discussed, highlighting methodological considerations for equity-focused psychological research. These methods can ensure adequate power and representation when examining relationships between intersectional identities and psychological phenomena in online samples.

articles_hidden.title: Delayed Feedback Improves Learning in Individuals with Parkinson’s Disease
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Sucich; Christopher J. Cagna; Erica Weber; Ekaterina Dobryakova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Learning and memory deficits are common in Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Effectively processing performance-related feedback is integral to learning but is often impaired in PD. Delaying feedback presentation by 6 seconds has been shown to circumvent these deficits during incremental learning tasks. The potential learning benefits of longer feedback delays, however, are unknown. The current study examined the effects of a 6-second delay and a 25-minute delay on learning during a declarative memory task in individuals with PD. 

Methods: Thirty participants with PD completed a verbal paired-associates task, during which they learned word pairs via trial-by-trial accuracy feedback presented immediately after making responses (No Delay; ND), after a 6-second delay (Short Delay; SD), and after a 25-minute delay (Long Delay; LD). Mixed effects models examined the influence of feedback timing condition on both final test performance and on improvement in performance between the learning and test phases. Exploratory hierarchical mixed models with neuropsychological tests examined potential individual difference predictors of delayed feedback learning.

Results: Both SD feedback and LD feedback predicted significantly greater improvement in performance, compared to ND feedback. Better working memory performance on the Digit Span Backwards Test predicted significantly greater improvement from LD feedback.

Conclusion: Longer feedback delays improve learning during a paired associates word learning task in individuals with PD. Shorter delays previously demonstrated to benefit incremental learning may also benefit other forms of learning. Working memory capacity may be an important predictor of these learning benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Large Language Models for Test-Enhanced Learning: A Tutorial and Proof of Concept
articles_hidden.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Daryl Yu Heng Lee; Frederic Dick; Eva Lash; David Shanks
articles_hidden.abstract: Practice tests improve retention of studied information and enhance learning and retrieval of new information (test-enhanced learning; TEL). In five preregistered studies (total N = 623)—four online randomized experiments and one correlational classroom study with final-year psychology undergraduates—we examined whether large language models (LLMs; Gemini and ChatGPT) can generate practice tests that promote TEL and whether this use of LLMs can be feasibly incorporated into a classroom setting. LLM-generated multiple-choice tests with fixed feedback did not improve 2-day recall of a TED Talk relative to a control (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast, LLM-generated short-answer tests with personalized feedback significantly improved 7-day recall of an educational video relative to rewatching it (Studies 3 and 4), regardless of whether final test format matched that of the practice test. In the classroom study, participation in fortnightly LLM-generated short-answer tests (with personalized feedback) on lecture content was positively associated with graded assessment performance, and students’ attitudes towards this use of LLMs were generally favorable. Overall, we demonstrate that LLMs can substantially reduce the practical burden of implementing TEL, while maintaining sufficiently good question quality and enabling automated personalized feedback, and that this approach can be feasibly deployed in an undergraduate psychology class.

articles_hidden.title: Using Customised LLM-Based Chatbots in Psychological Research: A Practical Tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Hu Meilan; Gabriel Rongyang Lau; Adalia Yin Hui Goh; Samuel Rhys Cox; Louis Tay; Andree Hartanto
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots offer new methodological opportunities for psychological research by enabling scalable, standardised, and interactive research procedures. However, their usefulness depends on the researchers’ ability to customise, evaluate, and deploy them in ways that align with the methodological requirements of a given study. The current tutorial provides a practical, step-by-step framework for developing customised LLM-based chatbots for psychological research. We distinguish between no-code or low-code development approaches, including provider-hosted chatbot builders and visual or low-code programming platforms, and code-based approaches using proprietary model application programming interfaces (APIs) or locally hosted open-weight models. We compare these approaches in terms of technical expertise, behavioural and workflow control, study integration, cost, data governance, maintenance, and reproducibility. We also outline key components of the process of customising an LLM-based chatbot and illustrate deployment workflows across multiple platforms, including local desktop interfaces, messaging applications and survey platforms. Finally, we discuss key considerations for research ethics, privacy, data governance, security, transparency, and reproducibility, including recommendations for documenting and sharing chatbot configurations and study procedures. Through this tutorial, we aim to support researchers in integrating customised LLM-based chatbots into psychological research and in expanding the methodological possibilities available to them.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring What Matters: Development of the TRACE Measure (Trauma, Resilience and Adversity in Cultural Experiences)
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Pryce; Yaacov Petscher; Sarah O'Dell; Chelsey Bowman; Stephanie Curenton-Jolly
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose
The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) framework has been instrumental in understanding the long-term effects of childhood adversity but has been critiqued for its limited attention to cultural context and resilience. This study introduces and pilots the TRACE measure (Trauma, Resilience, and Adversity in Cultural Experiences), a culturally informed extension of ACE that integrates traditional adversity indicators, culturally specific adversities, and resilience factors within a single framework. The purpose of this study was to examine the preliminary psychometric properties and structural validity of the TRACE measure.

Methods
The TRACE measure was administered to parents (N = 122) of kindergarten students participating in a longitudinal literacy project across eight elementary schools. The instrument included three domains: traditional ACE items, culturally informed ACE (C-ACE) items, and culturally informed resilience (C-Resilience) items. Confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) using weighted least squares estimation (WLSMV) were conducted to evaluate dimensionality and model fit. Competing models, including correlated factors and bifactor structures, were compared. Reliability was assessed using coefficient omega (ω).

Results
Item-level CFAs demonstrated good model fit and strong reliability for both ACE (ω = .95) and C-ACE (ω = .93) domains, with acceptable reliability for C-Resilience (ω = .78). The correlated factors model showed poor fit, whereas bifactor models demonstrated improved fit, supporting a general adversity factor (G-ACE) alongside domain-specific factors. The general factor accounted for approximately 55%–59% of the common variance among adversity indicators. A moderate inverse relationship between adversity and resilience was observed (r ≈ −.50), indicating that these constructs remain distinct.

Conclusions
Findings provide support for the TRACE measure as a psychometrically viable and conceptually meaningful extension of the ACE framework. By integrating culturally informed adversity and resilience within a single instrument, TRACE offers a more comprehensive and contextual approach to assessing childhood experiences. This framework has implications for research, practice, and policy by supporting more culturally responsive and asset-based approaches to understanding and addressing childhood adversity.

Keywords: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Resilience, Cultural Contexts, Psychometrics, Trauma

articles_hidden.title: Youth Perspectives on Physical Activity Promotion in a Statewide 4-H Youth Development System
articles_hidden.authors: Denver M. Y. Brown; Amirhossein Ghanaatian; Peter Stoepker; Judith Sempa; Zaira Sandoval; Sarah Maass; Doina Caragea
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Cooperative Extension’s youth development program, 4-H, offers community-based infrastructure that may support physical activity (PA) promotion, particularly among rural youth, but youth perspectives on its role remain understudied. This study characterized youth perceptions of (1) how Kansas 4-H currently supports PA and (2) what additional PA opportunities the organization could offer. 
Methods: We analyzed responses to two open-ended items from a cross-sectional online survey of Kansas 4-H youth in Grades 3–12. Question-specific topic guides were developed through large language model (LLM)–assisted topic discovery and domain-expert finalization. Responses were coded by multiple open-weight LLMs, with human review of disagreement and quality-control cases. Exploratory subgroup analyses examined differences by rurality, gender, and grade.
Results: Among 710 respondents (52.5% female, 68.9% rural), the current-support and desired-opportunity items yielded 692 and 464 usable responses, respectively. Current supports most often involved livestock and animal care (40.0%), games, sports, and active recreation (35.4%), and hands-on projects, service, and active work (10.4%). Desired opportunities centered on sports and active recreation (29.5%); walking, running, hiking, and cycling (25.6%); and outdoor, adventure, and nature activities (9.5%). Subgroup differences were observed for livestock/animal care (rural vs urban: +10.2 percentage points), shooting sports/archery (male vs female: +5.4), and games/sports/active recreation (Grade 12 vs Grade 3: -14.0; all p≤.05).
Conclusions: Findings support a layered approach that integrates PA more intentionally into existing 4-H programming, while expanding opportunities responsive to youth interests and local resources. Community-engaged co-design can help translate these priorities into feasible programming across 4-H settings.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of a Mobile Recovery Support App on Substance Use and Related Consequences Among Adults Seeking to Maintain Sobriety: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph LaBrie; Bradley M. Trager; Weizhou Tang; Oliver Hatch; Kelsey Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: This study evaluated whether Pink Cloud, a mobile recovery support application, improves substance use outcomes among adults seeking to maintain sobriety. Method: Participants were 1,209 adults who reported abstaining from alcohol and other drugs for at least 72 hours. Participants were randomized to receive access to Pink Cloud or to an active control condition. Outcomes included the number of days participants used alcohol and/or drugs and the number of alcohol- and/or drug-related consequences experienced during the past 30 days (1-month follow-up) and the past 60 days (3-month follow-up). Hurdle models were conducted to examine condition differences in the likelihood of reporting any use or consequences and, among participants reporting each outcome, the number of days used or consequences experienced. Results: Across follow-up, participants assigned to Pink Cloud were significantly less likely than control participants to report any alcohol/drug-related consequences (OR = 0.75). Sensitivity analyses indicated that, at 1 month, Pink Cloud participants were significantly less likely to report any alcohol/drug use (OR = 0.77) and, among those who used, reported significantly fewer days of use (IRR = 0.79). They were also significantly less likely to report any alcohol/drug-related consequences at 1 month (OR = 0.72). Conclusion: Findings provide preliminary evidence that Pink Cloud may offer support for maintaining sobriety. Future research should determine whether mobile recovery support tools, such as Pink Cloud, can provide more sustained benefits when integrated with formal treatment, continuing care, and peer-based recovery support.

articles_hidden.title: The ordinary concept of intelligence is inclusive but hierarchical
articles_hidden.authors: carlotta pavese; Paul Henne
articles_hidden.abstract: A scientist solves a difficult problem. A footballer makes a decisive play. People may judge both intelligent, but are they equally inclined to infer that each person is intelligent? Across eight experiments and three supplementary experiments (N = 6,979), we found they were not.
