articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the potential benefits and barriers to the utilization of puppets within behaviour intervention of children during their pre-operational stage of development. It presents a  systematic qualitative review of studies that either aim to reduce antisocial behaviour or develop pro social behaviour. Works included educational and clinical settings and development of pro social behaviours such as inclusion and sharing, and reduction of anti-social behaviour such as refusal to comply and aggressive behaviours. The literature was searched using scholarly databases, with additional articles sourced from snowball method of similar reviews. Papers were included based on specific selection criteria and multiple validity and reliability measures. The wider field of research regarding puppetry within behaviour highlighted the overlap of socio-cognitive factors with the psychological principles and concepts of modeling, shared cognition, mediation and social influence being present among studies. From the review, utilizations of puppetry differed and overlapped among studies with modeling, mediation, performance and pedagogy all being utilized to develop and/or reduce behaviours. With majority of studies predominantly exploring the development of pro social behaviour, no significant differences between processes in reduction or development of behaviour were determined. Key themes among all studies were (1) internalization and interaction, (2) direct communication, (3) indirect communication, (4) play and indirect therapy, and (5) rehearsal and imitation. Benefits highlighted were the strengthened communication and dual development of three-party relationships in the sense that facilitators and researchers gained greater insight of participants’ perspective via indirect and direct communication, and vice versa. Though all studies reported positive behavioural change, there are barriers regarding the assessment of behavioural change and determination of purpose and intent.

articles_hidden.title: Epigenetic mechanisms of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review of Human and Preclinical Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: June Kang; JeYoung Jung
articles_hidden.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) produces clinical and behavioural effects persisting weeks to months beyond stimulation. This persistence is typically attributed to LTP- and LTD-like synaptic plasticity, yet short-lived synaptic events alone cannot explain it; epigenetic mechanisms, the leading candidate substrate, have never been systematically evaluated. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC to June 2026 (2,089 records; 1,941 de-duplicated). Twenty-two studies were eligible: ten human, ten preclinical, and two invasive cervical-VNS studies retained for sensitivity analysis. Among 18 interventional studies, 17 reported significant epigenetic change (94%; p = 1.45×10⁻⁴), driven by the controlled animal tier (10/10; p = 0.002); the human stream alone (5/6) was non-significant (p = 0.22). Adjusting for publication bias, the pooled signal held under a moderately conservative null (p₀ = 0.7, p = 0.020) but not a strongly conservative one (p₀ = 0.8, p = 0.15). Effects spanned histone modifications, DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and epigenetic enzymes. Histone acetylation was the most compelling pathway, supported by causal pharmacological rescue in rodent rTMS and tDCS models. DNA methylation showed an "epigenetic homeostat" pattern, normalising stress-induced aberrations at promoters including BDNF and COMT. Non-coding RNAs formed the largest stream, with circulating miR-146a-5p recurring across rTMS trials. BDNF emerged as a convergent node, also predicting rTMS response via baseline methylation and circulating microRNAs. Coverage is skewed: rTMS and tDCS dominate, tVNS is sparse, tACS/tRNS uninvestigated. NIBS is consistently associated with epigenetic remodelling across mechanisms and species, positioning chromatin regulation as a primary substrate for durable neuromodulatory after-effects.

articles_hidden.title: Antecedents of ecospirituality across cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Ira Billet; Adam Baimel
articles_hidden.abstract: The idea that humanity and nature are spiritually connected—ecospirituality—is a core aspect of cultural and religious worldviews around the world. Sociocultural factors, like religion, urbanization, and socioeconomic status, are hypothesized to shape people’s spiritual connections with nature, yet there are no systematic cross-cultural surveys of ecospirituality that can speak to these hypotheses. We present the results of a study assessing the associations between ecospirituality and these three sociocultural factors using a cross-cultural sample of religious individuals from 15 countries spanning the 5 major world religions (N = 11,186) and a sample of religious and non-religious individuals from the United States (N = 3,329). The overall pattern of results suggested that greater religiosity, urbanization, and socioeconomic status contribute to greater ecospirituality across cultural and religious contexts. Results in the sample of individuals in the United States largely departed from the results found across other countries in the cross-cultural sample, even other Western majority-Christian societies. This research contributes to our understanding of how sociocultural factors that are rapidly changing in many parts of the world may shape people’s connections with the natural environment.

articles_hidden.title: Disentangling between- and within-person effects of HIV PrEP and treatment attitudes on condom use and bacterial STIs among sexual minority men
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Adam Hart; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Yangqing Deng; Syed Noor; David M. Moore; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Daniel Grace; Nathan Lachowsky; Joseph Cox; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling
articles_hidden.abstract: HIV treatment attitudes and HIV PrEP are associated with sexual behavior that elevates the risk for bacterial STIs (B-STIs) among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Using a longitudinal multi-site study (Engage Cohort Study, 2017-2024), we modelled direct and indirect within- and between-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on condomless anal sex (CAS) and incident B-STIs among 1863 HIV-negative GBM. We modelled up to four years of follow-up visits using multi-level mediation analysis, with CAS as a mediating variable between HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs. We found direct within-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs, such that participants were more likely to report incident B-STIs at time points if they reported using PrEP and being more optimistic about HIV treatments; there were no indirect within-person effects through CAS. In contrast, we found both direct and indirect between-person effects. Specifically, participants who reported more PrEP use or who were more optimistic about HIV treatments over the course of the study were more likely to report incident B-STIs. Further, these effects were partially mediated by CAS. Given that we found within-person PrEP use is associated with increased CAS and STIs, and the general increase in adoption of PrEP over time, there is a need to expand biomedical intervention programs for B-STIs prophylaxis by integrating them with social and informational interventions about B-STIs risks, especially for GBM who use HIV PrEP.

articles_hidden.title: Is there a “shape bias” for places?
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Kirsten Mark; Moira Rose Dillon
articles_hidden.abstract: Early emerging biases support our learning of new words, like a tendency to extend novel nouns referring to objects to other objects of the same shape. The present work tests the generalizability of this “shape bias” in another foundational domain of everyday life — the domain of places. Adults and 6-year-old children, but not 3-year-old children, extended novel nouns to places of the same shape over places composed of the same-colored walls, regardless of whether places were described by novel nouns in labeling phrases or in more place-relevant prepositional phrases. All age groups, by contrast, showed a shape bias for objects that matched many features of the place stimuli. This relatively delayed shape bias for places suggests that at least some word-learning biases may emerge separately for different domains.

articles_hidden.title: Not all effort is equal: Invested and demanded effort in nicotine abstinence
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Wahlers; William Hart; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Katie Garrison; Seung-Lark Lim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Understanding the connection between perceived effort and nicotine abstinence requires recognizing not only how much effort people anticipate exerting, but why they anticipate exerting it. The Invested and Demanded Effort Model (IDEM) provides a framework for distinguishing between perceptions of effort associated with favorable and unfavorable psychological conditions for abstinence.

Method
E-cigarette users between the ages of 21 and 35 in the United States were recruited via Prolific (N = 253; Mage = 28.66, SDage = 4.22, 54.15% female, 45.85% male; 57.71% White, 20.16% Black, 9.09% Hispanic, 6.32% Mixed). We assessed anticipated invested and demanded effort toward nicotine abstinence (adapted Invested and Demanded Effort Scale [IDES]), states that make quitting feel difficult (e.g., e-cigarette dependence motivation, craving), goal-directed states that support quitting (e.g., cessation motivation), and abstinence-related traits (i.e., trait self-control, self-efficacy).

Results
Anticipated invested effort was associated with greater goal-directed states that support quitting including cessation motivation, cessation confidence, and willingness to bear the cost of abstinence whereas anticipated demanded effort was associated with greater states that make quitting feel difficult including e-cigarette dependence motivation, behavior, and craving and less willingness to bear the cost of abstinence. These findings were not attributable to confounding with trait self-control and self-efficacy.

Conclusions
Anticipated effort had no universal connection with abstinence-related states but depended on whether effortful control is attributed to one’s volition irrespective of self-control demands (invested effort) or the demands of abstinence (demanded effort). These findings bolster IDEM and extend its relevance to self-control contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Carrying the Hidden Stone: Mapping "The Sisyphean Quad" in Pre- and Posttrauma Discourses and Its Application
articles_hidden.authors: Swarnendu Karmakar
articles_hidden.abstract: This article introduces the Sisyphean Quad, a framework conceptualizing trauma as recursive and multidimensional across psychological, social, ethical, and existential domains. The model identifies four interlocking constructs: Sisyphean Burden (enduring moral, emotional, existential weight), Sisyphean Curve (cyclical fluctuations, nonlinear progression, unpredictable rhythms), Sisyphean Reflex (automatic survival responses, defense mechanisms, ingrained coping patterns bypassing awareness), and Sisyphean Paradox (tension between coping and preservation of identity). The recursive tightness of these constructs is captured by the Tono Factor (τ), approximated empirically by the Tono Index (τ^) via the Tono Scale (rating recurrence frequency, reflex rigidity, distress intensity, and recovery latency). To apply the model, this article also introduces the Triangular Model of Sisyphean Discussion integrates logotherapy for meaning; psychoanalysis for Burden, Curve, and Reflex; and Cognitive–Behavioral Pattern Interruption for resolution restructure of the paradox and future occurrence. Analyzing trauma across neurological, cognitive, behavioral, existential, cultural, and narrative layers, the article develops an ontologically stacked, interdisciplinary model, the first of its kind. Clinically, the Quad distinguishes maladaptive recurrence from meaningful return, guiding therapeutic dialogue when clients feel trapped in repeating patterns; reducing τ (and τ^) becomes the goal of intervention, loosening the cycle without erasing it. This theoretical and metatheoretical contribution introduces the Sisyphean Quad as a first universal account of trauma’s recursive architecture, where recurrence becomes not a failure but a gentle invitation to reenter life with renewed meaning and coherence.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a treatment pathway to reduce violence risk in psychosis:  from risk assessment to complex intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Whiting; Belinda Lennox; Seena Fazel
articles_hidden.abstract: Violence perpetration is an important adverse outcome for psychiatric services to reduce. Clinical services for psychosis, such as Early Intervention in Psychosis services, represent a key opportunity for prevention, but this is challenging without specialist expertise and resource for violence risk assessment and management. One innovation to address this is a scalable clinical prediction tool for violence, OxMIV, which has been developed using contemporary statistical approaches and been found to be both feasible to use and more accurate than clinical judgement alone in these settings. However, assessing risk does not reduce violence unless it leads to effective interventions being offered more consistently to those who are most likely to benefit. Evidence-based, population health approaches for linking individual risk estimates to intervention pathways have been successfully implemented elsewhere in medicine. Here we adopt such an approach for assessing and reducing the risk of violence in psychosis, presenting a framework for using OxMIV to support decision-making around allocating resources for further assessment and offering interventions that address modifiable risk factors. To develop, implement and test the effectiveness of such clinical pathways, assessments of risk and linked interventions should be studied together as complex healthcare interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Kudos to CUDOS: Resurrecting Mertonian Principles to Remedy Politicized Science
articles_hidden.authors: Cory J Clark; Medhini Urs
articles_hidden.abstract: Science is the most effective system humans have developed to understand reality. Like all systems, it is flawed and subject to bias and error. Reforms such as the Open Science movement seek to address these issues by institutionalizing long-standing Mertonian norms (communalism, universalism, disinterestedness, organized skepticism), helping scientists escape their biases and discover truth. However, other actions within scientific institutions have introduced ideological and political values into the truth-seeking domain, including harm-based censorship, DEI policies, positionality statements, and endorsements of political candidates and positions, among others. These developments can deprioritize epistemic quality and decrease public trust in science. Because the politicization of science arising within the academy has occurred primarily from one direction (i.e., left-wing), some strategies to counteract this bias have been to prioritize ideological/political diversity in hiring, or to encourage scientists to stay away from weighing in on political issues altogether. We argue that these well-meaning solutions to the problem of politicization compounds non-epistemic values in science, thereby risking further loss in public trust. Effort should be directed to restoring Mertonian norms that historically underpinned scientific credibility so that epistemic rigor can be improved and the issues of politicization can be solved without introducing more politics.

articles_hidden.title: Priority Maps, Featureful Processing, and the Superior Colliculus
articles_hidden.authors: Wayne Wu; Neeraj J. Gandhi; James P. Herman
articles_hidden.abstract: The priority map has been used to explain how locations are prioritized for attention and behavior. Priority maps provide a test case for how computational models and neural data can be integrated. Focusing on the superior colliculus (SC) as a paradigm neural substrate for priority maps, we raise two questions: (1) What does priority mean computationally? (2) Since priority maps are featureless, how can this be integrated with recent work on feature coding in SC? We argue that the priority map remains computationally unclear because the nature of priority remains unsettled. Given emerging evidence for “featureful” coding within SC, we challenge the priority map’s featureless assumption as applied to SC and suggest an alternative: a featureful priority matrix where feature dimensions remain distinctly represented.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Gino, Ayal, et al.’s (2009) Contagion and Differentiation in Unethical Behavior: A Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Esra Aslan
articles_hidden.abstract: Individual behavior is often shaped by observing others’ actions. The seminal Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) study found that individuals behave more dishonestly after witnessing blatant dishonesty by an ingroup member than by an outgroup member. However, because there was no group-irrelevant baseline condition, it remains unclear whether ingroup contagion, outgroup differentiation, or both drive the effect. Furthermore, using natural groups of university students leaves it unclear whether distinct properties of natural groups are necessary, or if mere categorization into arbitrary groups suffices. In this registered report, we tested Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) general hypothesis that exposure to ingroup dishonesty norms increases individual dishonest behavior more than exposure to outgroup dishonesty norms. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of their Experiment 1 with 3,323 U.S. Americans using both minimal and natural groups. Participants were exposed to standardized information about others' dishonest behavior, where we systematically varied the group identities of dishonest others. Then, they completed an incentivized coin-flip task where participants could double their earnings by lying. Despite manipulation checks suggesting that participants processed norm information and strongly identified with natural groups, the pre-registered ingroup-outgroup hypotheses were not supported. Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence for null effects across comparisons (BF₀₁ = 3.15-14.71). The core ingroup-versus-outgroup prediction received particularly strong null evidence (BF₀₁ > 14). We conclude that exposure to ingroup versus outgroup dishonesty norms, delivered through descriptive statistics in online settings, might not differentially affect individual dishonest behavior, revealing a boundary condition of the original finding.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles_hidden.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Attributed Innateness Beliefs Moderate the Heritability of Psychological Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Jern
articles_hidden.abstract:
People vary in how strongly they believe their psychological traits are innate. Using a 
twin/sibling design (N = 5,844; 1,043 MZ and 2,607 DZ families), I tested whether such 
beliefs moderate the heritability of 11 traits spanning sexuality, personality, attitudes, and 
health behavior. Innateness beliefs significantly moderated heritability for all traits: 
individuals who considered a trait more innate showed higher heritability for that trait. The 
effect was more trait-specific than indicative of a general essentialist tendency and largely 
driven by the individual's own belief rather than shared familial or genetic factors 
(religiosity and risk-taking were partial exceptions). A stringent sensitivity analysis reduced 
the number of significant traits from 11 to 6, indicating that for some traits the moderation 
may at least partly reflect a confound between extreme trait scores and innateness beliefs. 
The low heritability of innateness beliefs is consistent with largely non-genetic beliefs 
gatekeeping the expression of genetic variation.

articles_hidden.title: A Bayesian Structure Inference Account of Biases in the Formation and Updating of Group Moral Impressions
articles_hidden.authors: Jieyun Li; Fuying Chen; Yi Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluating a group's morality requires integrating its members' behaviors to form an impression, and updating these evaluations as new information emerges. We captured both impression formation and updating within a single Bayesian nonparametric framework: observers infer latent structures from group's behavioral distributions, thereby generating systematic biases in both static and changing contexts. During moral impression formation, when a group exhibits both common (dense) and rare (sparse) moral behaviors, the structure inference account (formalized by the Chinese Restaurant Process, CRP) predicts a sparsity bias, where rare behaviors trigger the inference of more latent structures. This opposes the "Common Is Moral" (CIM) heuristic, which predicts a density bias anchored to the high-frequency majority. Behavioral and computational modeling results (Experiments 1a-1b) showed a sparsity bias better explained by structural inference rather than frequency heuristics. Representational Similarity Analysis (Experiment 2) further revealed that observers' mental representations of groups organize around these inferred structures. Critically, moving to moral impression updating (Experiment 3), we found that impression biases track the shifting valence of newly sparse information. We captured the underlying structural evolution by extending the framework to changing environments via the Recurrent CRP (RCRP). Together, these findings suggest that the formation and updating of moral group impressions can be understood under a single cognitive perspective, implying that social biases could be mitigated by strategically altering information distributions.

articles.title: When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
articles.authors: Rithik Bhattacharjee
articles.abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.authors: Reza Ardekani Shaker; Justus Uitermark
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
articles.authors: Apeksha Shetty; Esther Simmendinger; Jula Lühring; Annie Waldherr; David Garcia; Hannah Metzler
articles.abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

articles.title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
articles.authors: Toby Hopp
articles.abstract:
Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM)
perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a
reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not
currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an
expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results
suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that
there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to
researchers.

articles.title: From Affective Experience to Mechanism: A Critical Realist Case Study Architecture Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis
articles.authors: Varun S. Nair
articles.abstract:
Studying affective life qualitatively poses a known problem. Burnout, emotional labour, and slow shifts in teacher–class relations are real with measurable effects, yet not directly visible; we infer them from behaviour and language. Interpretation always mediates. How can we claim mechanisms without pretending to observe them?
This paper proposes a case-study architecture using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist frame. It integrates five usually separate elements: a multi-perspectival case design; abduction and retroduction as genuinely different inferences; systematic assessment of rival explanations; a procedure for sorting context from mechanism when they do not separate cleanly; and a hierarchy of claims calibrated to evidence. The combination yields what neither purely interpretive nor purely causal work can: fallible mechanism explanations that take meaning and causation equally seriously.
The argument is specified, not demonstrated. Two computational simulations provide proof of concept. The first distinguishes two known ground-truth mechanisms across 40 synthetic cases, with 80% overall recovery (95% CI [68%, 92%]; 85% and 75% per mechanism). The second adds a third rival—perceptual reconstruction, in which teacher behaviour is unchanged but students report change—and distinguishes all three across 60 synthetic cases, with 95% overall recovery (100%, 100%, 85%). The three-way test uses tighter noise parameters than the two-way, so rates are not directly comparable. Both test only one component and neither substitutes for empirical validation on real classroom data, which remains future work.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: The Substitution Trap: Development Aid and the Composition of Government Spending in Indian States
articles.authors: Krishna Vadlamannati; Roberto Iacono
articles.abstract: The question of whether aid supplements or substitutes government spending has long been debated in public finance literature. Building on Vadlamannati and Iacono (2026), who examine how development aid affects discretionary fiscal transfers to Indian states, we address a distinct fiscal question: how does aid exposure affect the composition of subnational government expenditure? Using panel data for 30 Indian states over 1979-2019 (41 years) and an instrumental variable strategy addressing potential endogeneity, we find that greater exposure to aid is associated with a lower share of capital expenditure and a higher share of revenue expenditure. This pattern is consistent with substitution of externally aided projects for domestically financed spending. The effect however varies systematically with electoral incentives. In states with greater electoral competition, aid is more strongly associated with capital expenditure, suggesting that electoral incentives can encourage state governments to channel external resources towards visible capital investments. Our findings extend the evidence on fiscal consequences of aid in India from the allocation of intergovernmental discretionary transfers to the composition of state government expenditure. Our findings reveal that the developmental effects of aid depend not only on how resources reach subnational governments but also on how governments subsequently allocate them.

articles.title: The Unequal Toll of Loneliness on Electoral Participation: Longitudinal Evidence from The Netherlands
articles.authors: Francesco Marolla; Arturo Bertero; Cristiano Vezzoni
articles.abstract:
While declining turnout is often attributed to a lack of social integration, the political relevance of
subjective disconnection has only recently drawn scholarly attention. Using eleven waves of the
LISS panel in the Netherlands, we study how social and emotional loneliness relate to electoral
participation, net of objective social position and objective social integration. Lower self-reported
voting propensity is tied specifically to social loneliness, the perceived lack of a broader community
network, whereas emotional loneliness shows no independent association once the social facet is
accounted for. Separating stable between-person differences from within-person change, we find this
gap concentrated among citizens who are chronically high in social loneliness, while within-person
fluctuations show no association, indicating that the relationship is dispositional rather than situational
and consistent with a link between chronic loneliness and weaker voting habits. Crucially, the gap is
substantially narrower among citizens with greater education, political interest, and partisanship. The
participatory cost of loneliness is therefore unevenly distributed across the electorate, falling hardest
on citizens with the fewest civic resources.

articles.title: The Influencer I’ll Vote For: Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok
articles.authors: Marcos Echevarria-Eirea
articles.abstract: TikTok, and social media generally, continue to rise as important spheres of political communication and information. Mapping how political elites use these platforms thus remains consequential to our understanding of the political arena. However, due to its relative infancy, we have yet to thoroughly study these patterns on TikTok across countries. In response to this shortcoming, this paper introduces Mapping Politicians and Parties on TikTok (MPPTikTok), a dataset of TikTok accounts for national MPs and parties across 17 Western democracies, comprising over 2,190 usernames. Using these to collect ≈260,000 posts, I then describe the supply of content (presence and posting activity) and the engagement it receives across party families. Both radical party families are proportionally more present, post more, and receive more engagement than the Mainstream. The Radical Left leads most clearly in proportional presence and posting activity, while achieving engagement levels comparable to the Radical Right, with differences between them depending on the metric.

articles.title: Calibrating Synthetic Respondents: A Within-Persona Experiment on Public Reactions to Protest in Turkey
articles.authors: MEHMET FUAT KINA; Helin Yaren Ekmen
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents, yet the inference pipeline that turns a persona into a response is rarely calibrated for the population and outcome it is applied to. This study makes population- and outcome-specific calibration the research task itself. Using a nationally representative survey in Turkey as the benchmark, we construct persona-conditioned synthetic respondents for all 2,615 survey participants and search a structured space of persona content, sampling strategies, temperatures, model backbones, and prompt framings. Calibration is assessed against two held-out outcomes that carry the response structures on which social movement research typically rests, a rare binary measure of protest participation and a five-point attitude item, and the selected protocols differ between the two. We then run a within-persona synthetic experiment that places the same protest for Kurdish-language education in a political opportunity and a political threat context. The threat context lowers simulated movement legitimacy and willingness to attend, and the simulated contrasts differentiate by political orientation, ethnicity, and education in the directions theory anticipates. Calibration is a precondition for reading synthetic experiments, not a robustness check appended to them.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: The Politics of Threat Construction: Securitisation as a Site of Contestation in Georgia’s Public Sphere
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili; Zinaida Bechná; Kornely Kakachia
articles.abstract: Moving beyond studies on contemporary security challenges posed by information manipulation, economic coercion, and military pressure, this article problematises the securitisation of foreign interference narratives by political leaders through the case of Georgia (2023–2025). The analysis draws on 325 social media posts by high-level officials and ten in-depth interviews with civic actors resisting state narratives. It relies on securitisation theory to (1) examine how political elites frame domestic actors as instruments of the Western interference despite the country’s constitutionally anchored pro-European orientation and overwhelming public support for EU integration, and (2) explore how counter-securitisation unfolds among civic actors. The findings reveal a structured securitising narrative grounded in sovereigntist logic, invoking historical memory, identity threats, and conspiracy framings to delegitimise civic actors as rootless and foreign aligned. However, rather than generating stable audience acceptance this securitising move triggers counter-securitisation as civic actors contest the proposed threat hierarchy, reframe Russia and democratic backsliding as primary dangers, and additionally mobilise performative resistance through street protest. The analysis highlights the agency of civic actors who simultaneously occupy the positions of securitised subjects and a segment of the audience and complements post-structuralist understandings of the securitisation as a co-constitutive and iterative rather than a linear process.

articles.title: Long-Term Sequences of State-Building and Violent Conflict
articles.authors: Alexander De Juan
articles.abstract: A large body of research demonstrates that state capacity is an important correlate of intrastate conflict. However, similar levels of present-day state capacity can result from different historical trajectories of state-building. I argue that specific sequences of state-building can shape the risk of violent conflict in the long run: geographical obstacles can isolate territories from state-building processes for extended periods, strengthening non-state institutions. The risk of violence increases once the state has accumulated sufficient capabilities to close this state-building gap. The extension of authority into peripheral territories triggers resistance from among local elites that mobilize their constituencies against the central state. I exploit exogenous variation in early state-penetration in Nepal to investigate this argument. Areas located below the Himalayan foothills were heavily Malaria-infested preventing the state from establishing meaningful presence until the implementation of a malaria eradication program in the 1950/60s. I make use of this specificity in Regression Discontinuity (RD) estimations. The findings lend support to the primary arguments of the paper and underscore the role of long-term sequences of development.

articles.title: Rounding and the bill-size gradient in tipping
articles.authors: Toby Qin; Vrund Gurjar
articles.abstract: Restaurant tip percentages often decline as bills increase. Rounding is one proposed explanation because a fixed upward adjustment adds more to the tip percentage on a small bill. We examine how much of the observed decline can be explained by adjustments of up to one dollar. We analyzed 22,446 checks with positive recorded tips, no automatic gratuity and bills of $10–$200 from three North Carolina restaurant outlets. For checks with a whole-dollar tip or reconstructed final payment, we allowed the pre-rounding tip to fall anywhere from one dollar below the recorded amount to the recorded amount, with a minimum of zero. We calculated the smallest and largest bill-size coefficients across these possible amounts, controlling for outlet, month, guest count, opening hour and weekday. Bootstrap checks resampled dates, weeks and servers. Each scheme used 999 draws, with the rounding bounds recalculated for each resampled dataset. Tip percentages fell by 4.29 points per bill doubling. Even the adjustments that most reduce this decline leave a coefficient of −1.62 points, which remains negative across all three bootstrap checks. Five-dollar rounding or restricting bills to $30–$200 allows the fitted decline to disappear. Upward dollar rounding cannot fully explain the negative gradient in the primary sample. Larger rounding increments and the exclusion of small bills produce ranges containing zero.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: Distributed Citizenship in Local-Oriented Online Communities: A Behavioral Repertoire of Civic Roles Across 50 North American City Groups
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities increasingly serve as informal spaces where residents exchange local knowledge, discuss public issues, and encounter local news. Yet existing research often treats these communities as digital third spaces, with less attention to how civic labor is distributed among participants. This study understands these communities as components of local information infrastructures, examining how civic roles are distributed by analyzing year-long data from 50 highly active North American city subreddits in 2024. Focusing on 43,263 sustained users, we combine media-domain matching, LLM-assisted topic classification, latent profile analysis, and qualitative case comparison. The analysis identifies six behavioral civic roles: National News Commentators, Platform-Native Political Discussants, Local Civic Respondents, Cross-Scale Media Brokers, Local News Brokers, and Peripheral Generalists. The findings show that local-oriented online communities function as local information infrastructures which depend on uneven but complementary forms of resident participation.

articles.title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
articles.authors: Monica Heilman
articles.abstract: Debates persist on the racial position of multiracial Americans, namely whether this population will “become White” or not. However, the premise of this question is predicated on a monoracial paradigm of race that cannot fully account for the experiences of multiracial individuals. Multiracial experiences with Whiteness, including ways they conform to and confound monoracial expectations, have the potential to reshape our understandings of racial constructions, boundaries, and futures, particularly considering shifting racial demographics. One necessary precursor toward these insights lies in the distinctions between how multiracial and monoracial individuals experience Whiteness. Drawing on thirty-seven in-depth interviews with multiracial young adults with White ancestry in the Midwest, I argue that multiracial individuals experience Whiteness as a wage (privileges) and a tax (costs). Like monoracial Whites, multiracial individuals viewed as White can receive public and psychological wages, yet these wages are offset by an inseparable “racial tax,” which is predicated on the contingent and exclusive nature of Whiteness. These results underscore the utility of calling attention to the monoracial structure, as well as recognizing and theorizing beyond its limits.

articles.title: Antagonistic Predictions
articles.authors: Christoph Kern
articles.abstract:
Why do we use models to predict the most likely outcome? Integrating model predictions into high-stakes decision-making pipelines can amplify biases and introduce flawed decisions when human caseworkers and models compete over the same prediction target. Learning to anticipate the most likely outcome risks reproducing biases embedded in historical data, while delivering such predictions in human-AI decision-making raises issues of cognitive biases and algorithmic aversion versus overreliance. 

In this perspective, I argue for Antagonistic Predictions, a structurally different paradigm where models are tasked to act as sparring partners that challenge human pre-conceptions and show reachable futures rather than anticipating the most common pattern. I envision instantiations of Antagonistic Predictions that can counteract historical disadvantages, social stereotyping, and cognitive biases and sketch potential implementations in predictive ML and generative AI settings.

articles.title: Who Sees Politics in Sports? Norm Endorsement and Partisan Judgments from the 2026 World Cup
articles.authors: Morgan Wack; Daniel Vogler; Manuel Arrigo; Christian Pipal; Lucas Paulo da Silva
articles.abstract: Most Americans say politics should stay out of sports. Yet whether this norm is truly binding depends on whether people apply it when their own side violates the norm. To test this "apolitical sports" norm, we fielded a two-wave matched panel survey around the 2026 FIFA World Cup (N1=988; N2=699). During the tournament, U.S. President Donald Trump called FIFA to have an American player's red-card suspension lifted. We asked respondents to judge the incident directly and to judge a message on players' shirts, varied to support or protest a contentious U.S. policy. Overall, endorsing the norm predicted lower tolerance for political expression in sports, within each party separately, with a smaller own-side advantage. Following this widely reported violation, Democrats raised their endorsement while Republicans did not. What divided partisans most was what they counted as a violation, with Republicans reporting less political interference. In short, while both sides agreed with the norm, they disagreed about whether it had been broken. Our findings suggest that partisan accommodation can influence how citizens recall and conceive of potentially norm-violating events.

articles.title: Different spaces, different citizens? Explaining online and offline volunteering and citizenship behavior through the Civic Voluntarism Model
articles.authors: Arjen de Wit; Marlou Ramaekers; Stephanie Maas; Rene Bekkers
articles.abstract: Online ways of communication have radically changed the face of volunteerism, often described as ‘virtual volunteering’, ‘online volunteering’ or ‘digital volunteering’. In this paper we examine if those individuals engaged in online spaces, both in formal organizations and in self-organized communities, are different from those engaged in offline (in-person) volunteering. To understand how the four distinct types of voluntary participation (offline volunteers, online volunteers, offline self-organized citizens, online self-organized citizens) attract the same or different individuals, we anchor our analysis in the Civic Voluntarism Model (CVM). Using panel survey data from the Netherlands, we find that offline and online volunteers show higher engagement and especially networks, and this also holds for people who participate as citizens in their neighborhood. ‘Being asked’ to volunteer is the strongest correlate of volunteering, both offline and online, as well as offline citizenship. Recruitment networks are less important for online participation. Strikingly, online self-organized platforms are able to reach new groups of citizens that are not stratified by similar prerequisites for participation. These findings provide valuable insights for volunteer managers, activists, and policy makers who use online channels to recruit and retain volunteers.

articles.title: What Affective Polarization Is Made Of: Components, Targets, Cleavages and Emotions in Five Multiparty Democracies
articles.authors: Mabelle Kretchner; Bendegúz Plesz; Eran Halperin; Julia Elad-Strenger; Sivan hirsch hoefler; Adva Gruenwald; Zsolt Boda
articles.abstract: The more affective polarization (AP) is studied, the clearer it becomes that a single score conceals what it is made of. The score has two sides, ingroup attachment and outgroup hostility, and the two need not be balanced. AP runs toward different targets, it runs along a different divide in each system, and the affect itself is made of distinct emotions. Comparative work has taken up each of these layers, but in the studies we are aware of, never all together, so what any given score is made of is still not known: two democracies with similar AP levels may be facing quite different things. Drawing on preregistered survey data from five multiparty democracies (Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Israel; N = 5,151), we map all four layers in one design: AP and its two sides toward parties, voters, and ideological blocs; where attachment and hostility sit across the parties of each system; and the associations of six discrete emotions with AP. In all countries, AP drew more on ingroup attachment than on outgroup hostility, and disappointment and anger rather than hatred were associated with AP toward parties and voters. What differed was where the affect settled: which parties concentrated it, and whether the ideological bloc carried it at all. Hatred appeared only at the bloc level and only in some systems, at the target whose scores were otherwise among the lowest. We discuss the importance of unfolding these layers together in comparative research, for a better understanding of AP and for addressing it.

articles.title: Between Finality and Accuracy: Vote Recount Institutions in European Democracies
articles.authors: Ivan Jarabinský; Patrik Mikóczi
articles.abstract: Vote recounts sit at the intersection of vote counting, dispute resolution, and post-electoral procedure, yet comparative knowledge of how democracies actually conduct them remains scarce. Drawing on a structured, focused comparison across ten European democracies that operate single-instance electoral judiciaries, we examine the institutional settings within which recounts take place. We frame the observed variation through what we term the finality-accuracy dilemma, the tension between treating certified results as settled and ensuring that declared results faithfully reflect voter preferences. Five dimensions structure our analysis, namely standing, threshold conditions, decision-making body, scope, and procedural deadlines. We identify five recurring configurations and find that decision-making body type aligns systematically with position on the finality-accuracy spectrum, with judicial bodies clustering on the finality side and parliamentary bodies adopting accuracy-leaning flexibility. No sampled system employs automatic margin-based triggers, and ordered recounts were partial rather than comprehensive in scope.

articles.title: Resilience in a Hybrid Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a hybrid security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: Designing social tipping interventions: a systematic framework for scaling up behavioural change
articles.authors: Gian Luca Pasin; Giulia Andrighetto; Eugenia Polizzi di Sorrentino; vito trianni
articles.abstract: Social tipping, the process by which a new behaviour spreads rapidly upon reaching a critical mass, offers a promising pathway for large-scale behavioural change. However, systematically designing interventions to trigger such tipping points remains a key challenge. This paper introduces a two-phase framework to guide researchers and policymakers in developing effective social tipping interventions. The first phase involves assessing the potential for social tipping by evaluating the prevalence of the target behaviour and the underlying preferences and social expectations that sustain it. We propose a  method for eliciting individual thresholds for changing behaviour, distinguishing between conditional subjects (those who require social proof for changing behaviour) and unconditional subjects (those who are independent of others' decisions). The second phase uses the diagnostic information to inform strategic decisions about whom to target and how to intervene to activate the social tipping process. We analyze the trade-offs between targeting different subpopulations (e.g., amenable vs. resistant individuals) and propose a “stepping stone” approach that breaks down change into manageable steps, which can be particularly effective in populations with polarized individual thresholds. Taken together, our framework offers a roadmap for scaling up large-scale behavioural change through social tipping.

articles.title: Genital Modifications and Moral Boundary-making: Medical Perspectives on FGM/C versus FGCS in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Hannelore Van Bavel
articles.abstract: This chapter investigates how medical professionals who perform female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) in Belgium and the Netherlands perceive and negotiate the boundary between FGCS and female genital mutilation (FGM). It draws on in-depth qualitative interviews conducted with 11 medical professionals between March 2024 and August 2025, as part of a broader study of genital self-image, motivations for FGCS, and clinical responses. FGM is criminalised in both countries, whereas FGCS is not, even though some procedures classified as FGCS technically fall within the legal and policy definitions of FGM. In 2008, professional societies in the Netherlands attempted to clarify the distinction but ultimately failed to establish concrete criteria, relying instead on what they regarded as a self-evident difference. Healthcare professionals are therefore left to interpret and navigate this boundary in practice, drawing on their own professional knowledge, moral reasoning, and sociocultural understandings. This ambiguity raises important questions about how medical professionals distinguish between FGM and FGCS in their everyday practice. Do they regard the two as fundamentally different, or do they recognise areas of overlap, and on what grounds? What forms of reasoning, knowledge, and professional or cultural frameworks inform their distinctions? To what extent do their views reflect, reproduce, or resist broader social, cultural, and political discourses?

articles.title: Insights from Facilitator Reflections and Participant Feedback: A Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training Model
articles.authors: Kate Dunne; Tara Doherty; Sinéad Hanrahan; Ruth Moran; Lorna Walsh; Caragh Tisdall; Ciara McManus; Seán Lacey
articles.abstract: The Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training (CIRIT) consortium was established in 2021 by representatives of Irish Research Performing Organisations (RPOs) to collaboratively develop and deliver research integrity (RI) and open science training across the Irish research sector. Underpinning the CIRIT model is a virtue-based approach to RI in which participants work in small groups to engage in dialogue and reflect on moral conflicts and authentic research dilemmas using problem-based learning (PBL) and social constructivist pedagogy. This exploratory mixed-methods case study examined the effectiveness of the CIRIT model and explored its potential as a collaborative cross-institutional approach to RI training. CIRIT facilitators acted as insider researchers, conducting two post-seminar dialogical reflections over a twelve-month period. Seminar participants completed an anonymous post-seminar feedback questionnaire following five CIRIT workshops. A Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) framework informed the analysis of the dialogical reflections, while questionnaire findings were used to contextualise and complement the facilitators' reflections. Findings indicate that the CIRIT model successfully fostered participant engagement, dialogue, and reflective discussion while supporting the development of a collaborative RI community of practice. The findings suggest that collaborative cross-institutional, virtue-based approaches offer a promising model for strengthening RI training and provide a transferable framework that could be adapted within other national research systems, while highlighting the importance of adequate resourcing and institutional recognition.

articles.title: Соотношение финансового и реального секторов как драйверов развития экономики: систематизация теоретических моделей в рамках 9-слойной схемы системы разделения труда // The Relationship between the Financial and Real Sectors as Drivers of Economic Development: Systematization of Theoretical Models within a Nine-Layer Scheme of the Division of Labor
articles.authors: Maksim Tsepkov
articles.abstract:
This meta-research is devoted to the systematization and conceptual comparison of key economic concepts that consider either the real sector and technological innovation, the financial sector, or state institutions as the fundamental drivers of economic development. Comparing traditional models is complicated by the fact that most authors focus on individual factors, ignoring complex interrelated relationships.

To overcome this limitation, nine-layer scheme of the division of labor of Petr Shchedrovitsky is used as an integrative analytical framework, encompassing levels from natural resources and production technologies to knowledge accumulation institutions and monetary systems. The study spatially visualizes the theoretical perspectives of Karl Marx, R. Hilferding, V. Lenin, J. Keynes, H. Minsky, J. Schumpeter, and C. Perez, as well as those of Latin American structuralism, Japanese "knowledge capitalism," and the Chinese school of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Positioning these concepts on a single map allows us to demonstrate their mutual complementarity at different phases of technological and financial cycles and lay the foundations for the synthesis of a comprehensive socioeconomic theory.

The study also identified four main phases of technological and economic cycles, during each of which the role of the financial sector shifts from stimulating to destructive. It is shown that state and national-institutional mechanisms (the Chinese model, the Japanese J-firm) are capable of blocking the speculative separation of the ninth layer from the real sector.

articles.title: The China Mirror  Learning through Difference in the Digital Age
articles.authors: Stéphane Grumbach
articles.abstract: Under conditions of rapidly increasing societal complexity, understanding other civilizations might become an epistemological necessity for fostering adaptive capacities. Drawing on Weber's Verstehen, Jullien's method of the écart, Luhmann's theory of observation, and Koselleck's conceptual history, we propose a method of differential displacement to compare not simply different situations, but their dynamics, with the aim of exposing implicit assumptions. As a case study, following Jullien, we examine what the categories through which China approaches the digital transformation can reveal to Europeans about its purposes and governance. The goal is neither to endorse nor to criticize China, but to move beyond the simplistic duality of democracy and authoritarianism and examine what the difference reveals about Europe's own categories. We further argue that persistent misunderstanding of others can progressively feed a misunderstanding of one's own transformation. Under conditions of complexity surge, comparison can become a mechanism of collective intelligence and adaptive learning.

articles.title: Disaggregating the AI elite: Gender, age, and education differences among professionals engaged in AI development
articles.authors: Matti Nelimarkka
articles.abstract: Amid the society-wide onrush of artificial intelligence, asking ‘who creates AI?’ holds great urgency. A questionnaire-based study conceptualising ‘AI elite’ as a narrower group than the conventionally considered ‘coding elite’ found that only 5% of the 16,808 engineering and technology professionals surveyed contributed significantly to their organisation’s projects for AI development, design, or deployment, with an additional 15% contributing somewhat. Examining predictors of AI-elite membership, path analysis revealed organisation position to be the strongest, suggesting a Matthew-effect pattern wherein pre-existing power informs control over AI. Gender shapes membership directly and indirectly (through education choices and access to senior positions), compounding women’s under-representation. Education likewise manifests both direct and mediated positive effects. Counter to expectations, variety in one’s everyday application of AI tools correlated negatively with participation in AI development. This evidence that the AI elite reproduces structural inequalities spotlights ramifications that warrant further research and well-targeted diversification efforts.

articles.title: An Overview of Public Administration Research: Insights From Publications in Leading Journals (2000–2024)
articles.authors: Vener Garayev
articles.abstract: This study examines paradigmatic changes, thematic developments and authorship patterns in public administration research by analyzing 4,317 articles published in Public Administration Review, Public Management Review, and Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory between 2000 and 2024. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques through Python software to analyze content of titles, abstracts, and metadata, the article identifies key thematic clusters and paradigmatic shifts across the period, shaped by global events, contextual challenges, and technological advancements. The findings reveal a transition from bureaucratic efficiency to participatory governance, from reform to resilience, and from administrative theory to data-driven governance. Additionally, analysis of authorship patterns reveals increasing collaboration and concentration of scholarly output among top prolific contributors. This study contributes to a growing body of literature on bibliometric and content analytical studies in public administration, offering a comprehensive, data-driven perspective on the field’s intellectual evolution over the past quarter-century.

articles.title: Building Bridges Through Infrastructure: Citizen Science and Institutional Integration in Air Quality Monitoring
articles.authors: Henri de Ruiter; Kirsten Vegt; Hester Volten; Margaret Gold; Janneke Elberse
articles.abstract: Citizens are increasingly using low-cost sensors to measure their surroundings, for example air quality. Sensor measurements offer greater temporal and spatial resolution and therefore have the potential to complement official monitoring practices. However, the integration of citizen science (CS) data into official frameworks is still limited. CS data are often perceived as “messy”, with barriers such as concerns about data quality, the absence of standard methodologies, and perceptions of unreliability. While these challenges are well-documented, the critical role of infrastructure in bridging CS data and institutional frameworks has received less attention. This study examines the case of Measure Together, a government-funded project and community that functions as a boundary organisation to bridge the gap between CS initiatives and institutional air quality monitoring. We explore how a CS infrastructure emerges through a combination of relational, organisational and technical factors aimed at making sense of CS data. We further analyse how this CS infrastructure is beginning to merge with official monitoring infrastructure, resulting in a hybrid infrastructure that seeks to combine local data and insights from CS with the standardised and rigorous approaches of official monitoring. Our analysis highlights critical tensions, including conflicts between local and generic data, the action-oriented expectations of many CS participants versus the long-term timelines of official infrastructure, and challenges around trust and standardisation. We conclude by identifying pathways to navigate these tensions, emphasizing the need for adaptive, participatory infrastructure that balance rigour with societal relevance, fostering greater integration between CS and official infrastructures.

articles.title: Dangers  of  non-objective constructions and  interpretations of history: Important assertions and  takeaways from an Indian context
articles.authors: Sujay Rao Mandavilli
articles.abstract:
This short and very brief paper in a way extends our previous papers and publications on historiography, 
though it is in many ways quite important to our core mission. Its importance cannot also not be 
discounted based on our general observation that non-objective and non-purposeful constructs of 
history are widely prevalent across the intellectual spectrum, and both from the left and the right, and 
various errors of omission and commission to this effect and deeply and foundationally entrenched. 
Therefore, it goes without saying that course-corrections are in order, and that the dangers of non
objective and highly biased and prejudiced constructs of history, especially those driven and propelled 
by ideology must be driven home to the broader and larger public. These assume added importance and 
significance in the Indian context for several reasons. Firstly, it precludes a scientific temper being 
inculcated among the laity, as they cannot trust mainstream scholarship any longer. Scientific constructs 
of history are also so important to relegate religion to the background eventually, and keep it in its 
place. Such constructs also lead to a culture of non-objectivity becoming deeply entrenched and it 
invariably begets counter-reactions from other ideologically driven groups. In addition, it is bound to 
severely compromise interdisciplinary approaches and integration across multiple periods and 
geographies all of which are so essential to the healthy growth of scholarship. In situations and 
circumstances where there are ideologically-driven ding dong battles as is presently the case, we may 
even need to adopt an outside in approach and educate the general public about non-objective and 
non-scientific constructs of history first. We are also at a loss to understand why a culture of service of 
historians to science, society, and the education system is not well-entrenched, and immediate course
corrections are in order to promote objectivity in mindset at all costs, and under all circumstances.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Calling Capitalism and Class in the United States: From Reconstruction and the Gilded Age to the Present
articles.authors: George Skouras
articles.abstract: This article explains how American capitalism repeatedly transformed rather than displaced the moral language of calling. Beginning with Reconstruction and the Gilded Age, it traces how disciplined labor, self-command, thrift, and achievement were detached from Calvinist theology and reembedded in corporations, schools, professions, credit systems, welfare institutions, and digitally mediated workplaces. It develops an institutional account of moralized inequality: institutions distribute unequal resources and opportunities, then classify unequal outcomes as individual merit, responsibility, or failure. The analysis distinguishes property, organizational authority, expertise, income, wealth, employment security, debt exposure, and institutional dependence, while showing how race, gender, citizenship, education, occupation, and locality convert historically unequal resources into apparently individual merit. Calling persists as a contested moral infrastructure of capitalism. The central question is whether institutions that demand effort, commitment, and self-investment can justify the unequal security, authority, wealth, and recognition that follow.

articles.title: Revisiting Social Media’s Emotion-Engagement Affinity: Audiovisual Evidence from Political Communication on TikTok
articles.authors: Marcos Echevarria-Eirea
articles.abstract: Despite considerable research on the use of emotion in online political communication, prior studies have largely relied on textual data. By focusing on TikTok, a highly audiovisual platform, this letter revisits the classic emotion-engagement affinity of social media by incorporating visual and audio components. Drawing on a large dataset of TikTok posts by politicians and parties in eight Western democracies, I test how multimodal emotional content associates with user engagement across different political ideologies. Results show that negative and high-arousal posts are associated with higher engagement across emotional forms. Although extremist and populist actors upload negative content more frequently, mainstream actors benefit just as much from an emotional communicative strategy.

articles.title: “TikTok refugees”: Motivations and political correlates of international platform migration
articles.authors: Yibin Fan; Hai Wang
articles.abstract: This study investigates the motivations and political correlates of large-scale platform migration in a transnational context. While prior research has emphasized social and technological drivers, the political significance of migration remains underexplored. Building on theories of alternative political expression, political and media trust, and political efficacy, this study conceptualizes platform migration as an alternative political expression. Using an online survey of a group of users with sustained adoption of RedNote, we analyze the case of “TikTok refugees,” examining five motivational mechanisms – social influence, platform-use orientation, political expression, cultural openness, and collective identity frames – and a series of political characteristics with migration.
